AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

Driven by record demand for AMD's EPYC server processors, Ryzen CPUs, and Instinct accelerators, the company's revenue totaled $10.253 billion, slightly down quarter-over-quarter (QoQ), but up significantly year-over-year (YoY). Furthermore, AMD raised its long-term outlook for the server CPU market, expecting it to reach $120 billion by 2030 due to increased demand from AI and agentic AI workloads. At the same time, the company admitted that sales of its AI accelerators were down sequentially. For the quarter ending March 28, AMD generated $10.253 billion in revenue, down slightly from $10.270 billion in the fourth quarter, but up 38% compared to $7.438 billion in the first quarter of 2025. The company's GAAP net income nearly doubled to $1.383 billion from $709 million as its gross margin hit 53%, up 3% YoY. Operating income rose 83% year-over-year to $1.476 billion. "We delivered an outstanding first quarter, driven by accelerating demand for AI infrastructure, with Data Center now the primary driver of our revenue and earnings growth," said Dr. Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. "We are seeing strong momentum as inferencing and agentic AI drive increasing demand for high-performance CPUs and accelerators. Looking ahead, we expect server growth to accelerate meaningfully as we scale supply to meet demand." While traditionally the lion's share of AMD's revenue came from selling processors and system-on-chips (SoCs) for client devices, in the recent years the company's data center segment delivered the bigger portion of the company's revenue while also showing rapid growth. In the first quarter, AMD's data center division earned $5.8 billion in revenue (up 57% year-over-year) and $1.6 billion in operating income (up from $900 million a year ago). AMD said server CPU sales increased more than 50% from the same quarter last year, with both cloud and enterprise demand growing over 50%. Lisa Su said AMD is seeing significantly higher CPU demand because AI workloads increasingly require CPUs for orchestration, data movement, head-node operations, and agentic AI execution. As a result, AMD now expects the server CPU market to grow at more than 35% annually through 2030 (compared to its prior forecast of around 18% CAGR), reaching $120 billion in 2030. In fact, the company expects sales of its EPYC processors for data centers to increase 70% year-over-year and sales of Instinct AI accelerators to be up 46% YoY in the second quarter.  "In response to this demand, we are working closely with our supply chain partners to meaningfully increase our wafer and back-end capacity to support this growth," Su said. "As a result, we now expect server CPU revenue to grow by more than 70% year-over-year in the second quarter, with robust growth continuing through the second half of 2026 and into 2027 as we ramp our next generation EPYC processors." AMD also revealed deeper engagement with major AI infrastructure customers. During the quarter, the company expanded its partnership with Meta , which plans to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs across several generations, including custom Instinct MI450-based accelerators integrated into AMD's Helios rack-scale AI platform. AMD said shipments tied to the Meta deployment are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2026. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. In addition, the company indicated that demand for its Instinct MI450-series accelerators and Helios systems from its alpha customer is already exceeding its initial expectations for 2027. Furthermore, multiple customers are now evaluating large-scale deployments for both training and inference workloads. "With this expanded visibility, we have strong and increasing confidence in our ability to deliver tens of billions of dollars in annual data center AI revenue in 2027 and to exceed our long-term growth target of greater than eighty percent in the coming years," Su said. At the same time, sales of AMD's Instinct accelerators — while growing 38% year-over-year — dropped slightly quarter-over-quarter due to lower sales to customers in China. Nonetheless, the company remains optimistic about Instinct's trajectory in Q2 and then in the second half of the year when the Instinct MI450-series starts to ramp. AMD not only set its own record in enterprise hardware sales during the quarter, but it continued to outsell Intel, which recorded $5.1 billion in revenue and $1.5 billion in operating income in the first quarter . When it comes to sales of client Ryzen CPUs, Radeon GPUs, and game console SoCs, AMD's revenue increased $3.6 billion, an increase of 23% year-over-year. Client revenue alone reached $2.9 billion, up 26%, driven by strong Ryzen processor demand and commercial PC share gains. Gaming revenue rose 11% to $720 million due to stronger Radeon GPU demand. " Semi-custom revenue declined year-over-year as expected at this stage of the console cycle, while engagements with customers on next generation platforms remain strong," said the head of AMD. "In graphics, revenue increased year-over-year, led by demand for our latest generation Radeon nine thousand series GPUs. AMD warned that both client and gaming revenue in the second half of the year would decline by more than 20% compared to the first half because of higher memory and component costs. " Similar to the PC market, we believe that second half demand in gaming will be impacted by higher memory and component costs, and we are planning the business accordingly," said Su. AMD's embedded revenue reached $873 million, up 6% year-over-year as industrial and edge demand improved. The business unit generated $338 million operating income, up from $328 million a year ago. The success of AMD's embedded division was driven by the company's strong positions across a variety of market segments that span from aerospace to communications and from defense to scientific applications. "Design win momentum for [embedded products] grew by a double-digit percentage year over year, with billions of dollars in new wins across markets, reflecting the continued expansion of our embedded business from a primarily FPGA-focused portfolio to a broader set of adaptive embedded x86 and semi-custom solutions, significantly expanding our TAM," said Su. AMD projects Q2 2026 revenue to reach about $11.2 billion ± $300 million. At the midpoint of the guidance, this would represent a 46% increase compared to the same period last year and about 9% growth sequentially. The company also expects non-GAAP gross margin to be around 56%. "[Q2 results will be ]driven by a very strong growth in our data center segment, [modest] growth in our client and the gaming segment, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment," said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, CFO and treasurer. For the quarter ending March 28, AMD generated $10.253 billion in revenue, down slightly from $10.270 billion in the fourth quarter, but up 38% compared to $7.438 billion in the first quarter of 2025. The company's GAAP net income nearly doubled to $1.383 billion from $709 million as its gross margin hit 53%, up 3% YoY. Operating income rose 83% year-over-year to $1.476 billion.

"We delivered an outstanding first quarter, driven by accelerating demand for AI infrastructure, with Data Center now the primary driver of our revenue and earnings growth," said Dr. Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. "We are seeing strong momentum as inferencing and agentic AI drive increasing demand for high-performance CPUs and accelerators. Looking ahead, we expect server growth to accelerate meaningfully as we scale supply to meet demand."

While traditionally the lion's share of AMD's revenue came from selling processors and system-on-chips (SoCs) for client devices, in the recent years the company's data center segment delivered the bigger portion of the company's revenue while also showing rapid growth. In the first quarter, AMD's data center division earned $5.8 billion in revenue (up 57% year-over-year) and $1.6 billion in operating income (up from $900 million a year ago). AMD said server CPU sales increased more than 50% from the same quarter last year, with both cloud and enterprise demand growing over 50%.

Lisa Su said AMD is seeing significantly higher CPU demand because AI workloads increasingly require CPUs for orchestration, data movement, head-node operations, and agentic AI execution. As a result, AMD now expects the server CPU market to grow at more than 35% annually through 2030 (compared to its prior forecast of around 18% CAGR), reaching $120 billion in 2030. In fact, the company expects sales of its EPYC processors for data centers to increase 70% year-over-year and sales of Instinct AI accelerators to be up 46% YoY in the second quarter.

"In response to this demand, we are working closely with our supply chain partners to meaningfully increase our wafer and back-end capacity to support this growth," Su said. "As a result, we now expect server CPU revenue to grow by more than 70% year-over-year in the second quarter, with robust growth continuing through the second half of 2026 and into 2027 as we ramp our next generation EPYC processors."

AMD also revealed deeper engagement with major AI infrastructure customers. During the quarter, the company expanded its partnership with Meta , which plans to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs across several generations, including custom Instinct MI450-based accelerators integrated into AMD's Helios rack-scale AI platform. AMD said shipments tied to the Meta deployment are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2026.

In addition, the company indicated that demand for its Instinct MI450-series accelerators and Helios systems from its alpha customer is already exceeding its initial expectations for 2027. Furthermore, multiple customers are now evaluating large-scale deployments for both training and inference workloads.

"With this expanded visibility, we have strong and increasing confidence in our ability to deliver tens of billions of dollars in annual data center AI revenue in 2027 and to exceed our long-term growth target of greater than eighty percent in the coming years," Su said.

At the same time, sales of AMD's Instinct accelerators — while growing 38% year-over-year — dropped slightly quarter-over-quarter due to lower sales to customers in China. Nonetheless, the company remains optimistic about Instinct's trajectory in Q2 and then in the second half of the year when the Instinct MI450-series starts to ramp.

AMD not only set its own record in enterprise hardware sales during the quarter, but it continued to outsell Intel, which recorded $5.1 billion in revenue and $1.5 billion in operating income in the first quarter .

When it comes to sales of client Ryzen CPUs, Radeon GPUs, and game console SoCs, AMD's revenue increased $3.6 billion, an increase of 23% year-over-year. Client revenue alone reached $2.9 billion, up 26%, driven by strong Ryzen processor demand and commercial PC share gains. Gaming revenue rose 11% to $720 million due to stronger Radeon GPU demand.

" Semi-custom revenue declined year-over-year as expected at this stage of the console cycle, while engagements with customers on next generation platforms remain strong," said the head of AMD. "In graphics, revenue increased year-over-year, led by demand for our latest generation Radeon nine thousand series GPUs.
AMD warned that both client and gaming revenue in the second half of the year would decline by more than 20% compared to the first half because of higher memory and component costs.
" Similar to the PC market, we believe that second half demand in gaming will be impacted by higher memory and component costs, and we are planning the business accordingly," said Su.

AMD's embedded revenue reached $873 million, up 6% year-over-year as industrial and edge demand improved. The business unit generated $338 million operating income, up from $328 million a year ago. The success of AMD's embedded division was driven by the company's strong positions across a variety of market segments that span from aerospace to communications and from defense to scientific applications.

"Design win momentum for [embedded products] grew by a double-digit percentage year over year, with billions of dollars in new wins across markets, reflecting the continued expansion of our embedded business from a primarily FPGA-focused portfolio to a broader set of adaptive embedded x86 and semi-custom solutions, significantly expanding our TAM," said Su.

AMD projects Q2 2026 revenue to reach about $11.2 billion ± $300 million. At the midpoint of the guidance, this would represent a 46% increase compared to the same period last year and about 9% growth sequentially. The company also expects non-GAAP gross margin to be around 56%.

"[Q2 results will be ]driven by a very strong growth in our data center segment, [modest] growth in our client and the gaming segment, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment," said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, CFO and treasurer.

sources.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
passages: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered.
AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs .
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion.
That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.
The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources.
There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business.
Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent.
AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

Article updated on October 27, 2026, 4:37 pm EDT It’s tough to pick smart home devices as gifts: Here’s what works the best. Smart home devices make some of the greatest gifts around — if you know how to pick them. The best gift choices are devices that are easy to understand and set up, don’t require any subscriptions or extra steps to use and offer real, useful benefits that won’t endanger anyone’s privacy. Oh, and if they’re easy on your wallet , that’s a plus. Here I’ve collected the smart tech I’ve tested that meets all the requirements for an excellent, memorable gift, including options for renters, older family members and those people who already seem to have everything. Take a look at security cams, app-connected heaters, wallet trackers, smart plugs and so much more to spice up this year’s gift giving. Note : The “smart” in smart home gifts refers to devices that typically require an app to operate or receive alerts. The good news is that many of them work with apps the recipient likely already uses, such as Apple Home, Google Home or Alexa. This robot vacuum comes from the first company to make them — iRobot. It was one of our top performers on hardwood floors, removing all the dust and debris, a bagless dustbin that can compress dirt for months of hands-free use, and saves you space since it doesn’t need a dock or base station. The mopping version is $450, but the vacuum-only model can usually be found for as low as $180. It’s a steal, whether it’s a gift for a loved one or yourself. Our experts have tested this product and selected it for this story. Its inclusion and description here solely reflect findings from our independent review. The company has paid for highlighted placements on this page. Upgrade your front porch security with Ring’s feature-packed battery-powered doorbell. The Ring Battery Doorbell 4K Pro delivers Retinal 4K video with a 10x enhanced zoom to capture clear, head-to-toe views of people on your doorstep day or night. It features radar-powered 3D motion detection for accurate movement alerts, color night vision and Live View with two-way talk so you can see and speak to visitors in real time. Setup is hassle-free, thanks to the quick-release ultrabattery pack that allows you to mount the unit anywhere around your home without standard hardwiring. The Shark StainForce is both a dry and a wet vacuum, small enough to hold in a hand but powerful enough to deal with tons of different fabric stains, especially with Shark’s stain-eliminating spray, which really impressed our reviewer, Ajay Kumar. Kumar tested the kit out on multiple pet stains, but it can work for just about anything, as long as users clean out the wet vac canister between uses. Oh, and did I mention the whole thing is entirely cordless? This pool robot represents the new age of pool cleaning , thanks to its AI navigation and its suction ability to collect leaves and even stones. David Watsky says it’s the most impressive out of all his tests, especially when it comes to its efficient three-hour battery life and the Patrol mode. Just make sure the recipient doesn’t already have a pool cleaning bot or has one so old that it desperately needs to be replaced. Home security cameras can be difficult to give as gifts since many are expensive and often come with subscription requirements to enable important features, such as cloud storage (which not everyone is comfortable with). But this Eufy camera solves all these problems. It’s affordable, supports local video storage with a microSD card and offers all features subscription-free, including human detection and privacy zones. The magnetic base is also easy to set up and to remove the camera from to recharge the camera as needed. It’s the best new cam I’ve tested to give as a gift for anyone interested in a security upgrade inside or out. You may want to bundle it with a microSD card so storage is taken care of, too. This high-tech smart lock is ideal for those who want to keep the look of a traditional lock but get smart features, including support for Apple Home Keys, Google Home, Alexa and more. No subscriptions are required, and the lock includes settings for remote locking, door status detection, auto locking and more. It also has an AAA rating from Builders Hardware Manufacturers Association, making it very durable. That makes it a particularly good gift to give someone who may not know much about smart homes but can appreciate an effective upgrade. However, I would bundle this with a Level Connect device to enable Wi-Fi, which is more or less necessary and will require an outlet somewhere in the house. Many security systems come with required subscriptions or contracts. This Aqara kit includes a 2K camera and several tiny sensors that work right out of the box, subscription-free. There’s a motion, vibration and door/window access sensor, which users can easily place wherever they want with the included adhesive strips and set up the app to get any extra any alerts. The camera can even enable AI recognition features with no extra costs, and serves as a hub so you can add more Aqara devices in the future. The kit even has somewhat limited support for Apple Home, Google Home and Alexa. extraction.body: It's hard to believe, but it's already time to start thinking about your holiday shopping. To answer this important question, we went to our team of experts, who tirelessly test hundreds of tech products each year, and asked them what they're thinking of gifting this year and, equally as important, what they'd like to receive. What you'll see below are not necessarily the top products of the year , but the ones we deem particularly gift-worthy. We've got the essentials like phones and PCs that just about anyone would appreciate. Our sibling sites are also hosting their own unique Gift of the Year awards. Check out the winners at CNET , Lifehacker , Mashable , Popular Science , and ZDNET for other fantastic holiday present ideas. —Eric Griffith You May Also Like Laptop Gift of the Year: Dell XPS 13 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Dell) Dell XPS 13 (2026) Review 4.0 Excellent $799.99 at Dell See It Looking to buy someone in your life an excellent laptop at an even more excellent price? Dell’s budget-focused reinvention of its iconic XPS laptop is one of the best laptops you can find for under $800. This 13-incher brings most of the luxury features you’ll find in costlier premium laptops, like a sharp, fast, and colorful touch screen, a snappy keyboard, and a slick, thin, and light chassis. We gave the Dell XPS 13 our Editors’ Choice award, and it’s by far the top Windows laptop to gift in 2026. —Joe Osborne Desktop Gift of the Year: Apple Mac mini M6 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Apple) Apple Mac mini (2026, M6) Review 4.0 Excellent $779.00 at Amazon $899.00 Save $120.00 See It The title of Mightiest Mini Desktop goes to the Apple Mac mini with M6. Yes, the memory shortage spurred a sizable price hike over the previous model, but the Mac mini is still the most powerful desktop you can get for less than $1,000. It boasts Apple’s most potent chip yet, which has an upgraded neural coprocessor, more advanced graphics, and faster memory bandwidth. Like most Macs, this one—an Editors' Choice—is ready for the long haul; it should last your lucky giftee a long time. —Joe Osborne Phone Gift of the Year: Google Pixel 11 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Google) Google Pixel 11 Review 4.0 Excellent $699.00 at Amazon $899.00 Save $200.00 See It With the Pixel 11, Google has slimmed down its Android phone and trimmed the camera bar, making the unit thinner and lighter. As a cherry on top, the Google phone offers 19 hours of battery life, so your giftee has no excuse for missing your texts. —Kimberly Gedeon TV Gift of the Year: Vizio Mini-LED Quantum TV (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Vizio) Vizio 65-Inch Mini-LED Quantum TV (VQM65C-1004) Review 4.0 Excellent $358.00 at Walmart $398.00 Save $40.00 See It The Vizio VQM-series Mini-LED Quantum TV is a dirt-cheap television that punches way above its weight in terms of performance. Plus, it supports both Apple AirPlay and Google Cast for streaming from your phone, tablet, or computer. This Editors' Choice set is a great package at under $280 for a 55-inch screen and under $800 for a massive 85-inch screen. —Will Greenwald Earbuds Gift of the Year: Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Anker) Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Review 4.0 Excellent $149.99 at Amazon $169.99 Save $20.00 See It The Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro midrange earbuds, which deliver effective active noise cancellation and a rich, bass-leaning sound profile for heavy music listeners, would make for the perfect stocking stuffer. The buds come in four colors, including pink and blue. —Florence Ion Smartwatch Gift of the Year: Apple Watch Series 12 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Apple) Apple Watch Series 12 Review 4.5 Outstanding Buy One Apple Watch, and Get a Second Apple Watch $300 off at T-Mobile See It The exceptional Apple Watch Series 12 puts the smart in smartwatch thanks to built-in Siri AI, which can answer the wearer's burning questions. It tracks your health with a brand-new sensing system that regularly checks your heart rate and other vital signs during and between workouts. Plus, this stylish device comes in multiple sizes, materials, and finishes, so you can perfectly tailor the look to fit your giftee. —Andrew Gebhart Health and Fitness Gift of the Year: Oura Ring 5 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Oura) Oura Ring 5 Review 4.0 Excellent $399.00 at Amazon See It The Oura Ring 5, an Editors' Choice, strikes the perfect balance between a stylish accessory and a useful health tracker. Even better, it lasts for over 10 days on a single charge. —Andrew Gebhart Smart Glasses Gift of the Year: Viture Beast (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Viture) Viture Beast Review 4.5 Outstanding $549.00 at Best Buy See It The Viture Beast is a pair of prism display glasses that you connect to any compatible phone, tablet, or computer via DisplayPort-over-USB-C to project a huge, private screen right in front of your eyes. The glasses also enable ultrawide 32:9 video with compatible devices, which I find vital when I’m trying to write and edit on the go. —Will Greenwald Recommended by Our Editors I Test Laptops All Year Long. These Are the 12 That Make My Holiday Gift List We Tested Them All: 100 Cost-Conscious Gifts You'll Love to Give Elevate Their Routine: The Best Tech Gifts for Health and Fitness Fans Ereader Gift of the Year: Onyx Boox Go 6 (Gen 2) (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Onyx Boox) Onyx Boox Go 6 (Gen II) Review 4.0 Excellent $199.99 at Amazon Check Stock If you know a power reader who gets their books from all sorts of sources—or just doesn’t want to use Amazon—Onyx Boox’s readers are a great alternative to the Kindle. There's a bit of a learning curve, but this is a powerful little E Ink tablet. —Will Greenwald Smart Home Gift of the Year: Birdfy Feeder Rookie (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Birdfy) Birdfy Feeder Rookie Review 4.5 Outstanding $69.99 at Amazon $109.99 Save $40.00 See It Shopping for your favorite birdwatcher? The Birdfy Feeder Rookie, an Editors' Choice, should be at the top of your list. We like the Rookie because its camera is much better than similarly priced alternatives. Make sure to get it with a bundled lifetime subscription; nobody likes getting a gift with a monthly fee. —Jim Fisher STEM Gift of the Year: DwarfLab Dwarf 3 Smart Telescope (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; DwarfLab) DwarfLab Dwarf 3 Smart Telescope Review 4.0 Excellent $549.00 at Amazon Check Stock Now this is an out-of-this-world gift. The affordable device weighs only 2.9 pounds and comes with a padded carrying case. (Tripod not included.) —Eric Griffith Under-$50 Gift of the Year: Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Razer) Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% Review 4.5 Outstanding $49.99 at Amazon See It If you’re looking for a present for that special nerd in your life and you don’t have a mint to spend, the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% is our top recommendation. This Editors' Choice is the best budget tenkeyless keyboard you can buy right now. —Zackery Cuevas

Article updated on October 27, 2026, 4:37 pm EDT It’s tough to pick smart home devices as gifts: Here’s what works the best. Smart home devices make some of the greatest gifts around — if you know how to pick them. Oh, and if they’re easy on your wallet , that’s a plus. Here I’ve collected the smart tech I’ve tested that meets all the requirements for an excellent, memorable gift, including options for renters, older family members and those people who already seem to have everything. The mopping version is $450, but the vacuum-only model can usually be found for as low as $180. It’s a steal, whether it’s a gift for a loved one or yourself. Our experts have tested this product and selected it for this story. Its inclusion and description here solely reflect findings from our independent review. The company has paid for highlighted placements on this page. Upgrade your front porch security with Ring’s feature-packed battery-powered doorbell. The Ring Battery Doorbell 4K Pro delivers Retinal 4K video with a 10x enhanced zoom to capture clear, head-to-toe views of people on your doorstep day or night. It features radar-powered 3D motion detection for accurate movement alerts, color night vision and Live View with two-way talk so you can see and speak to visitors in real time. Setup is hassle-free, thanks to the quick-release ultrabattery pack that allows you to mount the unit anywhere around your home without standard hardwiring. The Shark StainForce is both a dry and a wet vacuum, small enough to hold in a hand but powerful enough to deal with tons of different fabric stains, especially with Shark’s stain-eliminating spray, which really impressed our reviewer, Ajay Kumar. Kumar tested the kit out on multiple pet stains, but it can work for just about anything, as long as users clean out the wet vac canister between uses. Oh, and did I mention the whole thing is entirely cordless? This pool robot represents the new age of pool cleaning , thanks to its AI navigation and its suction ability to collect leaves and even stones. David Watsky says it’s the most impressive out of all his tests, especially when it comes to its efficient three-hour battery life and the Patrol mode. Just make sure the recipient doesn’t already have a pool cleaning bot or has one so old that it desperately needs to be replaced. Home security cameras can be difficult to give as gifts since many are expensive and often come with subscription requirements to enable important features, such as cloud storage (which not everyone is comfortable with). But this Eufy camera solves all these problems. The magnetic base is also easy to set up and to remove the camera from to recharge the camera as needed. It’s the best new cam I’ve tested to give as a gift for anyone interested in a security upgrade inside or out. You may want to bundle it with a microSD card so storage is taken care of, too. This high-tech smart lock is ideal for those who want to keep the look of a traditional lock but get smart features, including support for Apple Home Keys, Google Home, Alexa and more. No subscriptions are required, and the lock includes settings for remote locking, door status detection, auto locking and more. It also has an AAA rating from Builders Hardware Manufacturers Association, making it very durable. That makes it a particularly good gift to give someone who may not know much about smart homes but can appreciate an effective upgrade. However, I would bundle this with a Level Connect device to enable Wi-Fi, which is more or less necessary and will require an outlet somewhere in the house. Many security systems come with required subscriptions or contracts. This Aqara kit includes a 2K camera and several tiny sensors that work right out of the box, subscription-free. There’s a motion, vibration and door/window access sensor, which users can easily place wherever they want with the included adhesive strips and set up the app to get any extra any alerts. The camera can even enable AI recognition features with no extra costs, and serves as a hub so you can add more Aqara devices in the future. The kit even has somewhat limited support for Apple Home, Google Home and Alexa. I’m a fan of several smart thermostats currently on the market, but between high prices and more complex features, they don’t always make good gifts. This Ecobee model, however, is reasonably affordable and designed to be as simple as possible, while also working seamlessly with Siri, Alexa and Google. Ecobee says it can help save up to 23% on yearly heating and cooling costs, which lines up with my own experiences, too. Plus, most people can handle the installation themselves with a little wiring. There’s a Nest Gen 3 video doorbell , but I prefer this wireless second-gen model as a gift. You can place it anywhere — it works well against door trim — and angle it outward if needed, so it fits just about any porch. Plus, you still get Nest’s free features, including three hours of cloud video storage to review footage and that very handy package detection tool. Emporia’s smart plug is extremely affordable, priced at around $10. It provides useful smart features without taking up too much space, attention or setup time. Just plug it into an outlet and download the app. That app lets people track energy use from devices plugged into the smart plug, control it remotely and set schedules for activation. It’s a low-effort upgrade to lamps, indoor fountains, TVs that need to be off by a certain hour and all sorts of other home tricks. SwitchBot’s wallet tracker is shaped like a card and made to fit into the average wallet if there’s room. If there isn’t room, it can easily work in the pocket of a nice jacket, a suitcase, laptop bag, backpack or other belongings. There’s no subscription, the battery lasts for years and you get automatic alerts when you leave the item behind, as well as the ability to track it. I’ve been using it in my own wallet for a long time now. OLight’s flashlight is the light of the future. It’s supercompact and superdurable, and it has multiple modes, including a spotlight, floodlight, UV light to spot stains, laser pointer and soft moonlight mode for dark trails. The flashlight offers brightness levels that can reach up to 1,700 lumens and has multiple recharging methods. It’s an amazing add-on for traveling, camping or general home use, but it’s a bit too expensive for some people to buy for themselves, making it a great option for a special gift instead. Technically, smoke detectors should be replaced every 10 years or so. If you know someone who could benefit from a new smoke detector, they may appreciate this smart model. It works with the Ring app and Alexa, but can give voice alerts on its own. Users get app notifications when batteries are running low and other useful information, so they don’t have to interpret chirps. Professional fire monitoring is available for a fee, but it’s certainly not necessary. Smart light bulbs make a great gift for people who don’t have a smart home yet. They fit in standard sockets, use long-lasting, energy-saving LEDs and offer smart features such as remote control, scheduling (even when you’re away) and voice-assistant support. Affordable options such as this Wiz bulb also include full color settings, so people can choose any hue they want. I recommend the two-pack — one smart bulb feels a little lonely. I’ve tested many smart floodlights, and I especially love how you don’t need to worry about replacing these LED models very often, as it’s a chore. But my favorite is GE Cync’s four-quadrant floodlight, which can change to four different colors simultaneously for a variety of moods or party lighting. Add in the great app UI and music syncing features and it’s a complete, fun package. The Kelvin heater is unlike any heater I’ve tested — a slim, portrait-like device that hangs on a wall and uses radiant heat to warm up objects in a room. It’s app-connected for remote control and scheduling — that last part I really like because radiant heaters take a bit longer to heat up a room, and you can schedule the heater to turn on an hour or so before you’re active. A radiant heater doesn’t have the same fire dangers as other space heaters, so it’s also much safer to leave alone while it’s working. Just make sure the recipient has enough room on a wall for it. A smart garage is a surprisingly useful addition to a home, and with this controller, you don’t even need to replace your motor or rails. It allows you to control your garage with your phone, get alerts about its status and set schedules or automatic closing. It works with most garage doors built after 1993, but it’s a good idea to quietly check the make and model of the gift receiver’s garage before you buy. This leak detector doesn’t require any additional hubs or hoops to jump through: You just activate the battery, connect it to the app and put it where you’re worried about leaks, such as under sinks, by water heaters, by pipes that may burst in below-zero weather or behind toilets that sometimes misbehave. The app and siren will let you know if water starts leaking. Google’s latest smart home speaker has some of the best sound I’ve heard for anything in its size or price range, making it an excellent option for music, especially since it supports all the streaming services, including Spotify, Tidal and Apple Music. Gemini for Home can answer questions, schedule events, control devices and make reminders for free, and I don’t think the paid tiers with continued conversations or other AI capabilities are really worth it for the typical home. Just make sure a smart speaker and voice assistant is something the recipient is interested in before buying, as some people aren’t fans. The Echo Show 11 has an 11-inch screen, and Alexa can connect to everything from YouTube videos to your favorite streaming services to catch up on a show while you’re busy in the kitchen, garage, office or other places around the home. The speakers aren’t shabby either, so this touchscreen display can easily double as a speaker. The visual options for reviewing schedules, events, reminders and recipes are also very useful. If the person you’re thinking of has an Amazon Prime subscription, they can access Alexa Plus for free and the AI’s many additional capabilities, such as ordering from Uber or Grubhub. Zafro’s smart fan is one of our favorites, dishing out airflow over 40 feet while staying quiet. You can control modes, oscillation and even schedules with the app or voice commands. Our tests showed impressive results when it came to performance, and we really like extras such as the easy-wash design as well as the ability to automatically turn the fan on based on its internal temperature sensor. A pet water fountain is already a good idea, since pets are more attracted to moving water. But this smart version is the best I’ve tested, with two separate tanks and a tray to avoid recirculating water, so it stays fresh much longer. It’s also very smart, including app controls that allow you to adjust refills and other details, even heating the water up for especially picky pets. But that’s only the beginning: This fountain also includes a pet camera that can identify pets when they approach and notify you when they’re drinking. It’s low to the ground, so it’s not a big privacy issue, but gives a person extra eyes on their pet, along with a two-way audio option to talk. There’s a subscription for video logs and other features, but I don’t think it’s necessary on this do-it-all model. Just keep in mind, it’s not really suited for especially large dogs. The Litter-Robot 5 is incredibly powerful and smart, easily enough to handle multiple cats. It comes with auto-scooping, app controls and a rounded design meant to help with cat safety, although older cats may need a ramp up to it. Not everyone likes all the smart features such as sensors, waste identification AI cameras and so on, many of which require a subscription to use, but if you’re looking for a simpler version of this product to give as a gift, we also really like the Whisker Litter-Robot 4 model . extraction.body: It's hard to believe, but it's already time to start thinking about your holiday shopping. To answer this important question, we went to our team of experts, who tirelessly test hundreds of tech products each year, and asked them what they're thinking of gifting this year and, equally as important, what they'd like to receive. What you'll see below are not necessarily the top products of the year , but the ones we deem particularly gift-worthy. We've got the essentials like phones and PCs that just about anyone would appreciate. Our sibling sites are also hosting their own unique Gift of the Year awards. Check out the winners at CNET , Lifehacker , Mashable , Popular Science , and ZDNET for other fantastic holiday present ideas. —Eric Griffith You May Also Like Laptop Gift of the Year: Dell XPS 13 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Dell) Dell XPS 13 (2026) Review 4.0 Excellent $799.99 at Dell See It Looking to buy someone in your life an excellent laptop at an even more excellent price? Dell’s budget-focused reinvention of its iconic XPS laptop is one of the best laptops you can find for under $800. This 13-incher brings most of the luxury features you’ll find in costlier premium laptops, like a sharp, fast, and colorful touch screen, a snappy keyboard, and a slick, thin, and light chassis. We gave the Dell XPS 13 our Editors’ Choice award, and it’s by far the top Windows laptop to gift in 2026. —Joe Osborne Desktop Gift of the Year: Apple Mac mini M6 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Apple) Apple Mac mini (2026, M6) Review 4.0 Excellent $779.00 at Amazon $899.00 Save $120.00 See It The title of Mightiest Mini Desktop goes to the Apple Mac mini with M6. Yes, the memory shortage spurred a sizable price hike over the previous model, but the Mac mini is still the most powerful desktop you can get for less than $1,000. It boasts Apple’s most potent chip yet, which has an upgraded neural coprocessor, more advanced graphics, and faster memory bandwidth. Like most Macs, this one—an Editors' Choice—is ready for the long haul; it should last your lucky giftee a long time. —Joe Osborne Phone Gift of the Year: Google Pixel 11 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Google) Google Pixel 11 Review 4.0 Excellent $699.00 at Amazon $899.00 Save $200.00 See It With the Pixel 11, Google has slimmed down its Android phone and trimmed the camera bar, making the unit thinner and lighter. As a cherry on top, the Google phone offers 19 hours of battery life, so your giftee has no excuse for missing your texts. —Kimberly Gedeon TV Gift of the Year: Vizio Mini-LED Quantum TV (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Vizio) Vizio 65-Inch Mini-LED Quantum TV (VQM65C-1004) Review 4.0 Excellent $358.00 at Walmart $398.00 Save $40.00 See It The Vizio VQM-series Mini-LED Quantum TV is a dirt-cheap television that punches way above its weight in terms of performance. Plus, it supports both Apple AirPlay and Google Cast for streaming from your phone, tablet, or computer. This Editors' Choice set is a great package at under $280 for a 55-inch screen and under $800 for a massive 85-inch screen. —Will Greenwald Earbuds Gift of the Year: Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Anker) Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Review 4.0 Excellent $149.99 at Amazon $169.99 Save $20.00 See It The Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro midrange earbuds, which deliver effective active noise cancellation and a rich, bass-leaning sound profile for heavy music listeners, would make for the perfect stocking stuffer. The buds come in four colors, including pink and blue. —Florence Ion Smartwatch Gift of the Year: Apple Watch Series 12 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Apple) Apple Watch Series 12 Review 4.5 Outstanding Buy One Apple Watch, and Get a Second Apple Watch $300 off at T-Mobile See It The exceptional Apple Watch Series 12 puts the smart in smartwatch thanks to built-in Siri AI, which can answer the wearer's burning questions. It tracks your health with a brand-new sensing system that regularly checks your heart rate and other vital signs during and between workouts. Plus, this stylish device comes in multiple sizes, materials, and finishes, so you can perfectly tailor the look to fit your giftee. —Andrew Gebhart Health and Fitness Gift of the Year: Oura Ring 5 (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Oura) Oura Ring 5 Review 4.0 Excellent $399.00 at Amazon See It The Oura Ring 5, an Editors' Choice, strikes the perfect balance between a stylish accessory and a useful health tracker. Even better, it lasts for over 10 days on a single charge. —Andrew Gebhart Smart Glasses Gift of the Year: Viture Beast (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Viture) Viture Beast Review 4.5 Outstanding $549.00 at Best Buy See It The Viture Beast is a pair of prism display glasses that you connect to any compatible phone, tablet, or computer via DisplayPort-over-USB-C to project a huge, private screen right in front of your eyes. The glasses also enable ultrawide 32:9 video with compatible devices, which I find vital when I’m trying to write and edit on the go. —Will Greenwald Recommended by Our Editors I Test Laptops All Year Long. These Are the 12 That Make My Holiday Gift List We Tested Them All: 100 Cost-Conscious Gifts You'll Love to Give Elevate Their Routine: The Best Tech Gifts for Health and Fitness Fans Ereader Gift of the Year: Onyx Boox Go 6 (Gen 2) (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Onyx Boox) Onyx Boox Go 6 (Gen II) Review 4.0 Excellent $199.99 at Amazon Check Stock If you know a power reader who gets their books from all sorts of sources—or just doesn’t want to use Amazon—Onyx Boox’s readers are a great alternative to the Kindle. There's a bit of a learning curve, but this is a powerful little E Ink tablet. —Will Greenwald Smart Home Gift of the Year: Birdfy Feeder Rookie (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Birdfy) Birdfy Feeder Rookie Review 4.5 Outstanding $69.99 at Amazon $109.99 Save $40.00 See It Shopping for your favorite birdwatcher? The Birdfy Feeder Rookie, an Editors' Choice, should be at the top of your list. We like the Rookie because its camera is much better than similarly priced alternatives. Make sure to get it with a bundled lifetime subscription; nobody likes getting a gift with a monthly fee. —Jim Fisher STEM Gift of the Year: DwarfLab Dwarf 3 Smart Telescope (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; DwarfLab) DwarfLab Dwarf 3 Smart Telescope Review 4.0 Excellent $549.00 at Amazon Check Stock Now this is an out-of-this-world gift. The affordable device weighs only 2.9 pounds and comes with a padded carrying case. (Tripod not included.) —Eric Griffith Under-$50 Gift of the Year: Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% (Credit: René Ramos/PCMag; Razer) Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% Review 4.5 Outstanding $49.99 at Amazon See It If you’re looking for a present for that special nerd in your life and you don’t have a mint to spend, the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% is our top recommendation. This Editors' Choice is the best budget tenkeyless keyboard you can buy right now. —Zackery Cuevas

sources.title: Most Chicago voters said they want ShotSpotter back, but that’s unlikely to sway Mayor Johnson - Chicago Sun-Times
passages: More than 70% of Chicagoans expressed in an advisory referendum Tuesday that they want to bring back gunshot detection technology to fight violent crime and speed up emergency response time to gunshot victims, but the vote is unlikely to pressure Mayor Brandon Johnson into reviving it.
City Council members leading the charge for a ShotSpotter replacement told the Chicago Sun-Times that while they hope this time would be different, they don’t expect it will be.
Matt O’Shea said Snelling was a proponent of ShotSpotter, and acting Chicago Police Supt.
Fred Waller agreed “it’s a valuable tool” to alert police and shave potentially lifesaving minutes from emergency response times.
“The mayor is always talking about [how] he’s got a mandate from the residents of the city of Chicago.

Larry Snelling to sign a new contract with ShotSpotter, but Johnson declared the ordinance illegal — even after negotiating a costly extension to retain the technology through the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.
Johnson then launched an open competition to replace ShotSpotter.

sources.title: ELECTION CENTRAL: Chicago voters lean yes on gunshot detection, millionaires' taxes and Midway Blitz compensation - Audacy
passages: CHICAGO (WBBM NEWSRADIO) Chicago voters appear to have a clear answer to some of the city's longest-running political debates: Yes.
From bringing back gunshot detection technology to taxing millionaires and seeking compensation from Washington for the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
All five questions placed on the ballot by the city and Chicago Public Schools drew strong support.
Voters also weighed in on a separate Cook County millionaires' tax proposal.
The strongest support was for seeking federal compensation for costs and economic losses associated with Operation Midway Blitz.
Nearly 85% of voters favored the proposal, according to preliminary results from election authorities, with about 91% of the expected Chicago vote counted.
More than 80% supported using revenue from a millionaires' tax to fund public schools.
But none of the votes automatically changes policy.
The six questions are advisory, meaning elected officials aren't required to carry out the results.
Still, the margins could give Mayor Brandon Johnson, City Council members and state lawmakers a clearer picture of where voters stand on issues they've spent years debating.
The operation sparked protests, legal disputes and concerns among businesses in immigrant neighborhoods.

Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago's Great Cities Institute estimated that the first year of heightened federal immigration enforcement resulted in $1.26 billion in lost retail and restaurant spending across Cook County, along with $107 million in lost local sales-tax revenue.
The ballot question asked whether Chicago should seek compensation for lost tax revenue, public safety expenses and services provided to affected residents.
The result gives Johnson, who backed the referendum, a strong expression of support from voters who participated.
But it doesn't establish that Chicago is legally entitled to recover those losses or require the federal government to pay.
About 72% supported restarting the use of technology that alerts first responders when gunfire is detected.
He had campaigned on eliminating the system, citing concerns about its effectiveness and the police response to alerts.
Some aldermen, particularly those representing neighborhoods with high levels of gun violence, fought to keep it.
They argued the technology could help first responders locate shooting victims even when nobody called 911.
The vote wasn't specifically about reinstating ShotSpotter.
Johnson's administration announced plans in October to test a different system in six South and West Side police districts.

Six years after Illinois voters rejected a constitutional amendment allowing graduated income-tax rates, voters in Chicago and Cook County were again being asked whether wealthy residents should pay more.
The two questions were separate, even though both concerned raising additional revenue from high-income taxpayers.
The proposals have drawn support from Johnson and the Chicago Teachers Union.
Opponents, including business advocates and fiscally conservative groups, argue that higher taxes could discourage investment or prompt wealthy taxpayers to leave Illinois.
Chicago voters also appear open to giving major outdoor festivals a permanent home.
About 68% supported developing a dedicated festival and event venue, the smallest Yes majority among the five city and school district questions, but still a substantial margin.
The proposal follows years of complaints about major festivals taking over public parks.
Lollapalooza in Grant Park and Riot Fest in Douglass Park have prompted concerns about closures, damaged grounds and interruptions to neighborhood recreation.
There is no proposed location, price tag or construction plan.
In Aurora, voters faced a different kind of referendum, one that could change how residents hold their mayor accountable between elections.
Former Mayor Richard Irvin, who lost his reelection bid to John Laesch in April 2025, backed a proposal allowing voters to recall a sitting mayor.
Supporters argued voters should have a way to remove elected officials without waiting for another regular mayoral election.

extraction.body: From WAMU and NPR, 1A convenes a conversation about the most important issues of our time. Hosted by Jenn White. News from Chicago with WBEZ’s Lisa Labuz. More than 70% of Chicagoans expressed in an advisory referendum Tuesday that they want to bring back gunshot detection technology to fight violent crime and speed up emergency response time to gunshot victims, but the vote is unlikely to pressure Mayor Brandon Johnson into reviving it. It’s been three years since Johnson honored a campaign promise to progressive supporters by canceling the city’s contract with ShotSpotter, the technology he derisively called a “walkie-talkie on a stick.” Johnson and his backers viewed the technology as costly, ineffective and a contributor to overpolicing in Black and Brown communities where the majority of gun violence occurs. Afterward, the City Council empowered then-Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling to sign a new contract with ShotSpotter, but Johnson declared the ordinance illegal — even after negotiating a costly extension to retain the technology through the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago. Johnson then launched an open competition to replace ShotSpotter. SoundThinking, the company that owns ShotSpotter, was one of 15 firms responding to the request for information and one of nine companies responding to a follow-up request for proposals. Nothing has happened since then — even though the last two city budgets set aside a combined $13.9 million for the replacement technology. Another $5 million is included in Johnson’s reelection budget. City Council hearings have done nothing to pressure the mayor to deliver a replacement contract. Chief Procurement Officer Sharla Roberts was a no-show at the most recent hearing. She infuriated City Council members by sending a letter informing them that a pilot program was about to begin in six police districts: Wentwort, Calumet, Englewood, Deering, Ogden and Harrison. The mystery program will test a variety of ideas, including more violence intervention, “drone-based situational awareness, license plate recognition and incident response systems for evidence preservation.” Gunshot detection technology is only part of the pilot, officials said. Against that backdrop, an advisory referendum proposed by retiring 13th Ward Ald. Marty Quinn appeared on Tuesday’s ballot: Should the City of Chicago restart the use of gunshot detection technology that informs first responders when gunshots are detected?” The nonbinding referendum garnered 72% support — 447,475 of the 617,413 votes cast — for replacing the gunshot detection technology that Johnson eliminated. The City Council has a long history of using advisory referendum questions to crowd out more controversial ballot topics that could impact voter turnout. Most of the time, the results don’t translate into any governmental action. More than 80% supported using revenue from a millionaires' tax to fund public schools.
But none of the votes automatically changes policy.

The operation sparked protests, legal disputes and concerns among businesses in immigrant neighborhoods.

He had campaigned on eliminating the system, citing concerns about its effectiveness and the police response to alerts.

Opponents, including business advocates and fiscally conservative groups, argue that higher taxes could discourage investment or prompt wealthy taxpayers to leave Illinois.
Chicago voters also appear open to giving major outdoor festivals a permanent home.

There is no proposed location, price tag or construction plan.

Former Mayor Richard Irvin, who lost his reelection bid to John Laesch in April 2025, backed a proposal allowing voters to recall a sitting mayor.

More than 80% supported using revenue from a millionaires' tax to fund public schools. Roughly 74% favored charging owners of long-vacant commercial properties to support Chicago Public Schools, while 72% supported restarting gunshot detection technology. Even the proposal with the smallest majority, creating a permanent outdoor festival venue, had the support of more than two-thirds of voters. A separate Cook County advisory question proposing a 3% income-tax surcharge on millionaires, with revenue split between property tax relief and education, was also drawing strong support in early returns. But none of the votes automatically changes policy. The six questions are advisory, meaning elected officials aren't required to carry out the results. Still, the margins could give Mayor Brandon Johnson, City Council members and state lawmakers a clearer picture of where voters stand on issues they've spent years debating. Two years after Mayor Brandon Johnson ended Chicago's ShotSpotter contract, voters appear to favor giving gunshot detection technology another chance. About 72% supported restarting the use of technology that alerts first responders when gunfire is detected. Johnson ended the city's contract with SoundThinking, the company behind ShotSpotter, in September 2024. He had campaigned on eliminating the system, citing concerns about its effectiveness and the police response to alerts. Some aldermen, particularly those representing neighborhoods with high levels of gun violence, fought to keep it. They argued the technology could help first responders locate shooting victims even when nobody called 911. Ald. Marty Quinn, one of ShotSpotter's most persistent supporters, helped advance the ballot question. The vote wasn't specifically about reinstating ShotSpotter. It asked whether Chicago should resume using gunshot detection technology. Johnson's administration announced plans in October to test a different system in six South and West Side police districts. The referendum doesn't require the city to expand that pilot or restore its former contract. Of the five Chicago city and school district questions, the proposal to seek compensation from Washington drew the strongest support. Nearly 85% voted yes on whether Chicago should pursue federal reimbursement for costs and economic harm associated with Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration's immigration enforcement campaign in Chicago and its suburbs. The operation sparked protests, legal disputes and concerns among businesses in immigrant neighborhoods. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago's Great Cities Institute estimated that the first year of heightened federal immigration enforcement resulted in $1.26 billion in lost retail and restaurant spending across Cook County, along with $107 million in lost local sales-tax revenue. The ballot question asked whether Chicago should seek compensation for lost tax revenue, public safety expenses and services provided to affected residents. The result gives Johnson, who backed the referendum, a strong expression of support from voters who participated. But it doesn't establish that Chicago is legally entitled to recover those losses or require the federal government to pay. It's also unclear how much of the estimated regional economic damage the city could legally seek to recover. Six years after Illinois voters rejected a constitutional amendment allowing graduated income-tax rates, voters in Chicago and Cook County were again being asked whether wealthy residents should pay more. In Chicago, more than 80% supported using revenue from a surcharge on millionaires to increase funding for public schools. A separate Cook County question proposed a 3% surcharge on income above $1 million, with half the revenue going toward property tax relief and the other half toward public education. That countywide measure was also leading in the early returns, although a current combined total for Chicago and suburban Cook County was not immediately available. Opponents, including business advocates and fiscally conservative groups, argue that higher taxes could discourage investment or prompt wealthy taxpayers to leave Illinois. Another proposal to generate revenue for Chicago Public Schools was receiving strong support. About 74% of voters favored requiring owners of long-term vacant or undeveloped commercial and investment properties to pay an additional annual charge, with the money going toward CPS. Supporters say the proposal could provide another source of school funding while encouraging property owners to develop vacant land or buildings. Nicole Lee advanced the ballot question, arguing a permanent festival site could reduce those disruptions and potentially bring investment to another part of the city. From bringing back gunshot detection technology to taxing millionaires and seeking compensation from Washington for the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. All five questions placed on the ballot by the city and Chicago Public Schools drew strong support. Voters also weighed in on a separate Cook County millionaires' tax proposal. The strongest support was for seeking federal compensation for costs and economic losses associated with Operation Midway Blitz. Nearly 85% of voters favored the proposal, according to preliminary results from election authorities, with about 91% of the expected Chicago vote counted. More than 80% supported using revenue from a millionaires' tax to fund public schools. Roughly 74% favored charging owners of long-vacant commercial properties to support Chicago Public Schools, while 72% supported restarting gunshot detection technology. Even the proposal with the smallest majority, creating a permanent outdoor festival venue, had the support of more than two-thirds of voters. A separate Cook County advisory question proposing a 3% income-tax surcharge on millionaires, with revenue split between property tax relief and education, was also drawing strong support in early returns. But none of the votes automatically changes policy. The six questions are advisory, meaning elected officials aren't required to carry out the results. Still, the margins could give Mayor Brandon Johnson, City Council members and state lawmakers a clearer picture of where voters stand on issues they've spent years debating.

Two years after Mayor Brandon Johnson ended Chicago's ShotSpotter contract, voters appear to favor giving gunshot detection technology another chance. About 72% supported restarting the use of technology that alerts first responders when gunfire is detected. Johnson ended the city's contract with SoundThinking, the company behind ShotSpotter, in September 2024. He had campaigned on eliminating the system, citing concerns about its effectiveness and the police response to alerts. Some aldermen, particularly those representing neighborhoods with high levels of gun violence, fought to keep it. They argued the technology could help first responders locate shooting victims even when nobody called 911. Ald. Marty Quinn, one of ShotSpotter's most persistent supporters, helped advance the ballot question. The vote wasn't specifically about reinstating ShotSpotter. It asked whether Chicago should resume using gunshot detection technology. Johnson's administration announced plans in October to test a different system in six South and West Side police districts. The referendum doesn't require the city to expand that pilot or restore its former contract.

Of the five Chicago city and school district questions, the proposal to seek compensation from Washington drew the strongest support. Nearly 85% voted yes on whether Chicago should pursue federal reimbursement for costs and economic harm associated with Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration's immigration enforcement campaign in Chicago and its suburbs. The operation sparked protests, legal disputes and concerns among businesses in immigrant neighborhoods. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago's Great Cities Institute estimated that the first year of heightened federal immigration enforcement resulted in $1.26 billion in lost retail and restaurant spending across Cook County, along with $107 million in lost local sales-tax revenue. The result gives Johnson, who backed the referendum, a strong expression of support from voters who participated. But it doesn't establish that Chicago is legally entitled to recover those losses or require the federal government to pay. It's also unclear how much of the estimated regional economic damage the city could legally seek to recover.

Opponents, including business advocates and fiscally conservative groups, argue that higher taxes could discourage investment or prompt wealthy taxpayers to leave Illinois.

passages: Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, was up nearly 3% Wednesday afternoon, trading above $80,000 following the Democrats' midterm victory.
But everyday crypto investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately, experts tell CNBC Make It.

"Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," says Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University.

Newer crypto products, such as tokenized stocks and accounts that pay investors a yield on their cryptocurrency holdings, could face slower launches, additional restrictions or stronger investor protections as Democrats gain influence over crypto policy, he says.
With the midterm win, "the legislative agenda changes, oversight gets tougher and the assumption that Washington will keep making life easier for crypto becomes much harder to defend," says Katz.

extraction.body: Democrats' takeover of Congress in the midterm elections could reshape efforts to regulate cryptocurrency, potentially bringing stronger investor protections while slowing legislation favored by the industry. But everyday crypto investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately, experts tell CNBC Make It. Federal regulators appointed under President Donald Trump remain in place, and cryptocurrency trading will continue much as before. "Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," says Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University. The bigger question is whether lawmakers can agree on lasting rules for the industry — and how those rules could affect everyday investors. The legislation would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission greater authority over cryptocurrency trading while reducing the Securities and Exchange Commission's role in overseeing certain digital assets. The distinction matters because the SEC generally regulates securities, such as stocks, and requires companies offering them to disclose financial information and investment risks. The CFTC primarily oversees derivatives markets, including futures contracts, and has more limited authority over everyday cryptocurrency trading. The bill passed the House in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote, but failed to advance in the Senate in September 2026 on a 49-50 procedural vote. Democratic opponents argued the legislation could weaken investor protections by allowing some cryptocurrencies to avoid stricter SEC oversight, including disclosure requirements intended to help investors assess risk. "CLARITY is dead," Reiners says. Although the bill could still pass during the lame-duck session before the new Congress takes office in January, he considers that unlikely. Any future legislation would likely need to address Democrats' concerns about investor protections and conflicts of interest involving Trump's crypto businesses, says Martin Mulyadi, an accounting professor at Shenandoah University. "The election does not end crypto market-structure legislation; it changes the authors of the next draft," Mulyadi says. For everyday investors, the Democratic sweep is unlikely to change much about the cryptocurrencies they already own. But it could affect which new investment products become available, says Mike Katz, a digital assets specialist and financial services partner at law firm Manatt. Newer crypto products, such as tokenized stocks and accounts that pay investors a yield on their cryptocurrency holdings, could face slower launches, additional restrictions or stronger investor protections as Democrats gain influence over crypto policy, he says. With the midterm win, "the legislative agenda changes, oversight gets tougher and the assumption that Washington will keep making life easier for crypto becomes much harder to defend," says Katz. That said, the SEC and CFTC can continue developing crypto regulations without Congress. But those rules could be reversed by future administrations, says Marcel Miu, a certified financial planner and founder of Simplify Wealth Planning. "An agency's rules are much easier to reverse than laws, which is why the preferred pathway was the CLARITY Act," Miu says. Even so, tighter regulation wouldn't necessarily mean lower cryptocurrency prices, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising. Prices will continue responding to interest rates, investor demand and other market forces. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, was up nearly 3% Wednesday afternoon, trading above $80,000 following the Democrats' midterm victory. "Investors should really not try to predict what Washington is going to do," Mills says. "They should spend more time on what they own, where they own it, how much exposure they have to this market and how much they're able to lose." extraction.body: Democrats' takeover of Congress in the midterm elections could reshape efforts to regulate cryptocurrency, potentially bringing stronger investor protections while slowing legislation favored by the industry. But everyday crypto investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately, experts tell CNBC Make It. Federal regulators appointed under President Donald Trump remain in place, and cryptocurrency trading will continue much as before. "Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," says Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University. The bigger question is whether lawmakers can agree on lasting rules for the industry — and how those rules could affect everyday investors. The legislation would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission greater authority over cryptocurrency trading while reducing the Securities and Exchange Commission's role in overseeing certain digital assets. The distinction matters because the SEC generally regulates securities, such as stocks, and requires companies offering them to disclose financial information and investment risks. The CFTC primarily oversees derivatives markets, including futures contracts, and has more limited authority over everyday cryptocurrency trading. The bill passed the House in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote, but failed to advance in the Senate in September 2026 on a 49-50 procedural vote. Democratic opponents argued the legislation could weaken investor protections by allowing some cryptocurrencies to avoid stricter SEC oversight, including disclosure requirements intended to help investors assess risk. "CLARITY is dead," Reiners says. Although the bill could still pass during the lame-duck session before the new Congress takes office in January, he considers that unlikely. Any future legislation would likely need to address Democrats' concerns about investor protections and conflicts of interest involving Trump's crypto businesses, says Martin Mulyadi, an accounting professor at Shenandoah University. "The election does not end crypto market-structure legislation; it changes the authors of the next draft," Mulyadi says. For everyday investors, the Democratic sweep is unlikely to change much about the cryptocurrencies they already own. But it could affect which new investment products become available, says Mike Katz, a digital assets specialist and financial services partner at law firm Manatt. Newer crypto products, such as tokenized stocks and accounts that pay investors a yield on their cryptocurrency holdings, could face slower launches, additional restrictions or stronger investor protections as Democrats gain influence over crypto policy, he says. With the midterm win, "the legislative agenda changes, oversight gets tougher and the assumption that Washington will keep making life easier for crypto becomes much harder to defend," says Katz. That said, the SEC and CFTC can continue developing crypto regulations without Congress. But those rules could be reversed by future administrations, says Marcel Miu, a certified financial planner and founder of Simplify Wealth Planning. "An agency's rules are much easier to reverse than laws, which is why the preferred pathway was the CLARITY Act," Miu says. Even so, tighter regulation wouldn't necessarily mean lower cryptocurrency prices, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising. Prices will continue responding to interest rates, investor demand and other market forces. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, was up nearly 3% Wednesday afternoon, trading above $80,000 following the Democrats' midterm victory. "Investors should really not try to predict what Washington is going to do," Mills says. "They should spend more time on what they own, where they own it, how much exposure they have to this market and how much they're able to lose." sources.title: SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provide network technology for U.S. mobile service - CNBC
passages: SpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon , AT&T and T-Mobile .
Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year.
Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed.
Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit.
Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers.
The news sent shares of U.S. carriers reeling.
Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile.

"Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today, with an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead," Durga Malladi, an executive vice president at Qualcomm, said in the statement.
With Qualcomm, SpaceX will be using the chipmaker's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations to enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile.
SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone.
SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information.
Qualcomm has a long history of making chips for cellular networks, but is best known for making the modems and radios that go inside devices, not base stations for running a wireless network.
The company has targeted carriers and other infrastructure companies since it made a bigger push into the 5G infrastructure market in 2020 .
While SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm's technology to establish tens of thousands of new cell sites, it hasn't announced partners among cell tower companies or said how many new towers may be required.
SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at close to $2 trillion.

sources.title: Qualcomm to Build SpaceX Starlink Mobile 5G Network - Hoodline
passages: SpaceX has signed a multiyear deal with Qualcomm to supply the hardware and software behind a brand-new nationwide cellular network for its Starlink Mobile service, with construction on tens of thousands of cell sites expected to begin in 2027.
The agreement marks one of the biggest bets yet in Elon Musk's push to turn his satellite internet business into a full-fledged wireless carrier capable of competing with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.

Qualcomm described the arrangement as its largest 5G initiative to date, a notable claim given the chipmaker's history of infrastructure partnerships with carriers including Verizon, Dish and Vodafone, per the same CNBC report.

Per a Qualcomm announcement carried by Yahoo Finance, SpaceX has selected Qualcomm's Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms for Starlink Mobile's U.S. nationwide terrestrial 5G network, specifically the Dragonwing QRU100 and QDU100 platforms.
The network will rely on Massive MIMO radio units with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, a configuration the announcement says is central to the buildout.
Fierce Network reports that every planned site will be a macro cell rather than a small cell, a distinction that matters for coverage range and capacity in a nationwide network.
The division of labor is split cleanly between the two companies.

Light Reading adds that Qualcomm's contribution includes the chips that host critical software inside a radio access network's distributed units, the components that process signals close to the antenna.

PCMag reports that analysts have questioned the cost of building out a competitive network, estimating it could run into the tens of billions of dollars, on top of the need for additional wireless spectrum and new retail and customer-support operations.

An FCC document shows SpaceX filed an application in February 2023 seeking to modify its Gen2 Starlink license to deploy antennas capable of communicating with mobile devices in the 1429–2690 MHz range outside the United States and to operate in the 1910–1915 MHz range, though the filing excerpt does not indicate whether that request was approved.
CNBC reported, citing The Washington Post, that SpaceX was also looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar.
TechCrunch has also noted SpaceX's Starlink partnership with T-Mobile, part of a broader strategy of pairing satellite coverage with ground-based infrastructure.

CNBC reports that Starlink accounted for 36% of SpaceX's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit, underscoring how central the satellite unit has become to the company's finances even as it branches into traditional cell service.
