coreStoryFacts.text: SpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon , AT&T and T-Mobile .
Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year.
Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed.
Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit.
Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers.

Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile.

SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone.
SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information.

sources.title: Qualcomm to Build SpaceX Starlink Mobile 5G Network - Hoodline
passages: SpaceX has signed a multiyear deal with Qualcomm to supply the hardware and software behind a brand-new nationwide cellular network for its Starlink Mobile service, with construction on tens of thousands of cell sites expected to begin in 2027.
The agreement marks one of the biggest bets yet in Elon Musk's push to turn his satellite internet business into a full-fledged wireless carrier capable of competing with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.

Qualcomm described the arrangement as its largest 5G initiative to date, a notable claim given the chipmaker's history of infrastructure partnerships with carriers including Verizon, Dish and Vodafone, per the same CNBC report.

Per a Qualcomm announcement carried by Yahoo Finance, SpaceX has selected Qualcomm's Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms for Starlink Mobile's U.S. nationwide terrestrial 5G network, specifically the Dragonwing QRU100 and QDU100 platforms.
The network will rely on Massive MIMO radio units with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, a configuration the announcement says is central to the buildout.
Fierce Network reports that every planned site will be a macro cell rather than a small cell, a distinction that matters for coverage range and capacity in a nationwide network.
The division of labor is split cleanly between the two companies.

Light Reading adds that Qualcomm's contribution includes the chips that host critical software inside a radio access network's distributed units, the components that process signals close to the antenna.

PCMag reports that analysts have questioned the cost of building out a competitive network, estimating it could run into the tens of billions of dollars, on top of the need for additional wireless spectrum and new retail and customer-support operations.

An FCC document shows SpaceX filed an application in February 2023 seeking to modify its Gen2 Starlink license to deploy antennas capable of communicating with mobile devices in the 1429–2690 MHz range outside the United States and to operate in the 1910–1915 MHz range, though the filing excerpt does not indicate whether that request was approved.
CNBC reported, citing The Washington Post, that SpaceX was also looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar.
TechCrunch has also noted SpaceX's Starlink partnership with T-Mobile, part of a broader strategy of pairing satellite coverage with ground-based infrastructure.

CNBC reports that Starlink accounted for 36% of SpaceX's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit, underscoring how central the satellite unit has become to the company's finances even as it branches into traditional cell service.

The agreement marks one of the biggest bets yet in Elon Musk's push to turn his satellite internet business into a full-fledged wireless carrier capable of competing with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. According to CNBC , SpaceX struck the multiyear deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its U.S. mobile carrier, though financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. Qualcomm described the arrangement as its largest 5G initiative to date, a notable claim given the chipmaker's history of infrastructure partnerships with carriers including Verizon, Dish and Vodafone, per the same CNBC report. Bloomberg reported that Qualcomm and SpaceX have signed the pact and that Qualcomm will build tens of thousands of cell sites for the new 5G network. The network will rely on Massive MIMO radio units with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, a configuration the announcement says is central to the buildout. Fierce Network reports that every planned site will be a macro cell rather than a small cell, a distinction that matters for coverage range and capacity in a nationwide network. The division of labor is split cleanly between the two companies. Qualcomm will supply the Dragonwing platforms along with commercial-grade Layer 1 software, while, as Fierce Network's report notes, it will be up to SpaceX and its own team to handle Layer 2, Layer 3 and the higher-level network technologies that act as the system's brains. Light Reading adds that Qualcomm's contribution includes the chips that host critical software inside a radio access network's distributed units, the components that process signals close to the antenna. SpaceX's network is expected to include tens of thousands of sites. Deployment is slated to begin in 2027, with tens of thousands of sites built out over the course of the multiyear agreement, according to Qualcomm's announcement. CNBC reported, citing The Washington Post, that SpaceX was also looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar. TechCrunch has also noted SpaceX's Starlink partnership with T-Mobile, part of a broader strategy of pairing satellite coverage with ground-based infrastructure. The push into terrestrial wireless comes as Starlink has become an outsized part of SpaceX's business. CNBC reports that Starlink accounted for 36% of SpaceX's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit, underscoring how central the satellite unit has become to the company's finances even as it branches into traditional cell service. Light Reading has also reported that SpaceX was in talks with U.S. tower owners about gaining access to at least 80,000 sites. Not everyone is convinced the economics will be easy. PCMag reports that analysts have questioned the cost of building out a competitive network, estimating it could run into the tens of billions of dollars, on top of the need for additional wireless spectrum and new retail and customer-support operations. For context on the scale SpaceX would need to match, PCMag cites a March report for the Wireless Infrastructure Association estimating that T-Mobile has access to roughly 82,000 cell towers, AT&T to about 75,000 and Verizon to around 65,000. Regulatory filings suggest SpaceX has been laying groundwork for wireless expansion for years. An FCC document shows SpaceX filed an application in February 2023 seeking to modify its Gen2 Starlink license to deploy antennas capable of communicating with mobile devices in the 1429–2690 MHz range outside the United States and to operate in the 1910–1915 MHz range, though the filing excerpt does not indicate whether that request was approved. sources.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
passages: While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.” At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real.

“The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.” While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency.

Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack.
In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack.
“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos.

They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.” Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals.
Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated.

extraction.body: In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures. “This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says. Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31. “Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.” Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says. Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.” At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says. “The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice. Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes. Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.” While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year. Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post. If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

sources.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist - Ars Technica
passages: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday.
The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum.
Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page.
The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft.

Binance immediately initiated multiple containment measures, including suspending withdrawals to restrict further outflows, coordinating with partners to freeze affected tokens, and taking steps to revoke unauthorized permissions.
Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” Binance said.
“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time.
The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.”
Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

extraction.body: Techniques included laptop infections, compromised internal tooling, and fake job interviews. The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” a report on the company’s investigation to date said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident. The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.” Binance said that the first incident related to the compromise likely occurred in June, when an engineer downloaded a tampered version of Homebrew. The company linked to this incident reported in May, and its security team detected the compromised laptop, but only after the malware operators obtained information about the roles of the engineer and his related colleagues on the Binance wallet infrastructure team. In September, a separate engineer received messages through a legitimate job-hunting platform he was using. The message came from an individual posing as a project director looking to hire new employees. The purported project director arranged a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative and a second-round interview with the purported CEO of the fictitious company. During the first interview, conducted over a video platform, the purported HR representative shared a social media account that included personal photos and videos. The second interview took place over a social chat app. During it, the engineer was instructed to download an “assignment” that linked to a code repository containing malicious code that eventually executed on the engineer’s device during the setup process. “The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” Binance said. “The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.” On October 20, the attackers used the compromised engineer’s computer and an internal AI tool to take control of two other engineer devices, including the one previously targeted with the trojanized Homebrew installer. That engineer’s wallet contained a token granting access to a container deployment. Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses. Binance then received an internal alert regarding large-volume transfers and immediately began investigating. Binance hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to an attacker-controlled address. The attacker then used the signing service to exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization mechanism. EIP-7702 allows an account to delegate certain execution rights to a smart contract without exposing the private key. In this case, the attacker used that mechanism to give an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet. Binance immediately initiated multiple containment measures, including suspending withdrawals to restrict further outflows, coordinating with partners to freeze affected tokens, and taking steps to revoke unauthorized permissions. These efforts froze a total of $2.85 billion in assets. However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure.The attackers submitted 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account nonce and establish malicious delegation authorizations. Once established, these authorizations enabled the attackers to continue moving assets independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure. Binance needed additional transactions to revoke these on-chain authorizations. The containment process involved additional technical complexities. Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations. The team therefore developed and executed a specialized procedure to revoke these authorizations, which required additional time. Furthermore, suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not automatically invalidate existing on-chain authorizations. Separately, TRM Security said the attackers used various means to launder successfully transferred assets through the TRON and Ethereum blockchain networks. The methods included “a self-minted token and liquidity pool, a lending receipt token passed between wallets, and cross-chain swaps chained through two bridges.” TRM is tracking the North Korean hacking group under the name TraderTraitor. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack.
In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack.
“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos.

They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.” Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals.
Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated.

The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday.
The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum.
Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page.
The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft.

Binance immediately initiated multiple containment measures, including suspending withdrawals to restrict further outflows, coordinating with partners to freeze affected tokens, and taking steps to revoke unauthorized permissions.
Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” Binance said.
“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time.
The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.”
Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure.The attackers submitted 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account nonce and establish malicious delegation authorizations.

extraction.body: In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures. “This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says. Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31. “Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.” Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says. Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.” At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says. “The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice. Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes. Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.” While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year. Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post. If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

“Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.
Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year.
At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online.

While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.” At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real.
The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat.
“Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes.
It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack.
On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly.
“The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.
Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate.
“The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says.

“The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.” While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency.
Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.
Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea.
As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges.
Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated.

“In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries.
“They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

extraction.body: Techniques included laptop infections, compromised internal tooling, and fake job interviews. The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” a report on the company’s investigation to date said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident. The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.” Binance said that the first incident related to the compromise likely occurred in June, when an engineer downloaded a tampered version of Homebrew. The company linked to this incident reported in May, and its security team detected the compromised laptop, but only after the malware operators obtained information about the roles of the engineer and his related colleagues on the Binance wallet infrastructure team. In September, a separate engineer received messages through a legitimate job-hunting platform he was using. The message came from an individual posing as a project director looking to hire new employees. The purported project director arranged a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative and a second-round interview with the purported CEO of the fictitious company. During the first interview, conducted over a video platform, the purported HR representative shared a social media account that included personal photos and videos. The second interview took place over a social chat app. During it, the engineer was instructed to download an “assignment” that linked to a code repository containing malicious code that eventually executed on the engineer’s device during the setup process. “The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” Binance said. “The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.” On October 20, the attackers used the compromised engineer’s computer and an internal AI tool to take control of two other engineer devices, including the one previously targeted with the trojanized Homebrew installer. That engineer’s wallet contained a token granting access to a container deployment. Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses. Binance then received an internal alert regarding large-volume transfers and immediately began investigating. Binance hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to an attacker-controlled address. The attacker then used the signing service to exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization mechanism. EIP-7702 allows an account to delegate certain execution rights to a smart contract without exposing the private key. In this case, the attacker used that mechanism to give an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet. Binance immediately initiated multiple containment measures, including suspending withdrawals to restrict further outflows, coordinating with partners to freeze affected tokens, and taking steps to revoke unauthorized permissions. These efforts froze a total of $2.85 billion in assets. However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure.The attackers submitted 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account nonce and establish malicious delegation authorizations. Once established, these authorizations enabled the attackers to continue moving assets independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure. Binance needed additional transactions to revoke these on-chain authorizations. The containment process involved additional technical complexities. Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations. The team therefore developed and executed a specialized procedure to revoke these authorizations, which required additional time. Furthermore, suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not automatically invalidate existing on-chain authorizations. Separately, TRM Security said the attackers used various means to launder successfully transferred assets through the TRON and Ethereum blockchain networks. The methods included “a self-minted token and liquidity pool, a lending receipt token passed between wallets, and cross-chain swaps chained through two bridges.” TRM is tracking the North Korean hacking group under the name TraderTraitor. passages: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home.

The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more.
AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home.

extraction.body: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more. With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home. These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home. AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

sources.title: Google fixes Gemini’s biggest Google Home frustrations - Android Police
passages: Gemini should now also cut you off less than before while speaking, which has been a common complaint among Google Home users in the Gemini early access program.

Google's biggest problem is that they do not fix any of their apps / products they just sunset them and create a new product to replace the existing that is usually worse and lacks the full functionality of the original.
Google Assistant and Gemini is a perfect example.
Google took its time to bring Gemini to Google Home devices .
While the AI-powered assistant improves the smart home experience, it's not without issues.
So, when you ask the AI assistant to turn off the lights, it will only do so in your current home.
Earlier this year, Google made Google Home automations more powerful by adding 20 new starters , conditions, and actions.
It is now expanding on those capabilities with even more starters and conditions.
These include triggers such as when your security system is armed, when a device is plugged in, or when it's docked.
I've had an Alexa/Google home hybrid system for awhile now.
Alexa isn't perfect but is way better than the new Gemini so I've switched exclusively to Alexa since you can't even do continued conversations with Google now.
Some speakers work on some lights, some don't think anything has been configured.
The exact same voice command will trigger two different operations...
The most practical solution for me is to delete everything and start over.
But why in the world would I start over with Google?
I have invested a lot in Google Home, but bought a parallel HA hub last year and with every failed integration, I shift a little more over to it.
Until now, only those enrolled in the Public Preview could use the app to receive notifications, check battery status, manage passcodes, and schedule guest access.
You cannot access them through Ask Home or Help me create.
The best of Android Police, directly in your inbox.
The list of improvements is extensive and includes more reliable handling of commands related to notes, reminders, timers, and alarms.

How about this Google/Spotify: When I ask for a song, give me the most commonly played song, not some obscure, live bootleg version that has 9 plays total, 5 of which is me asking for the "album version" of the song.
The Google speakers are far superior at picking up voice commands across the room or when there is background noise like a TV.
You can also display custom cards on the Nest Hub screens.
But I do think it enhances HA capabilities by being linked to Google.
There may be improvements, but Gemini on home still sounds like a mess.
Even Gemini on my phone has told me it's a text based AI and is incapable of creating pictures when I've selected 'Create Image'.
Can't imagine it managing my smart home voice interactions.
Like the other commenter here, I went full bore with Home Assistant.
I watched for insights on whether Google learned its lesson, and they haven't, so we walked away.
Google didn't fire anyone in its product management team, so we put it all behind us.
After arguing with my google nest mini about its ability to broadcast for 15 minute last weekend I built a Home Assistant server and got my lights setup on it.
Anyone knows when Gemini wil come to South Africa?
I'm still standing in my bedroom in the dark repeating, for the fourth or fifth time, "Ok Google, turn on the bedroom light." While every other smart device in my home gets toggled on and off.

extraction.body: AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more. With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off. You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home. These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan. AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home. AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode. It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs, which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices. ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

While the AI-powered assistant improves the smart home experience, it's not without issues.
So, when you ask the AI assistant to turn off the lights, it will only do so in your current home.

I watched for insights on whether Google learned its lesson, and they haven't, so we walked away.

Gemini for Home will also be smart enough to use your saved home address when you ask questions like, “What’s the weather?” or catch up on local news. Gemini in Google Home will now also do a better job at differentiating between your multiple homes. So, when you ask the AI assistant to turn off the lights, it will only do so in your current home. Gemini should now also cut you off less than before while speaking, which has been a common complaint among Google Home users in the Gemini early access program. The full list of changes and improvements is as follows: If you’re a Google Home Premium Advanced subscriber, the new Live Search feature lets you use Gemini to get real-time updates about what’s happening in your home. It is now expanding on those capabilities with even more starters and conditions. These include triggers such as when your security system is armed, when a device is plugged in, or when it's docked. If you own a Nest x Yale Lock , Google is now expanding its support in the Google Home app to everyone. Until now, only those enrolled in the Public Preview could use the app to receive notifications, check battery status, manage passcodes, and schedule guest access. Google didn't fire anyone in its product management team, so we put it all behind us.
Like the other commenter here, I went full bore with Home Assistant. I watched for insights on whether Google learned its lesson, and they haven't, so we walked away.
Anyone knows when Gemini wil come to South Africa?

We really are living in the future we were promised.

The exact same voice command will trigger two different operations... Like a lot. The most practical solution for me is to delete everything and start over. But why in the world would I start over with Google? It's so disappointing. I have invested a lot in Google Home, but bought a parallel HA hub last year and with every failed integration, I shift a little more over to it.

sources.title: Bitcoin slips as Democratic sweep bets threaten crypto agenda - The Business Times
passages: BITCOIN edged lower as bets on a possible Democratic sweep of Congress gained traction , adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite.
For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment.
Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom.
Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets.
The original cryptocurrency slipped as much as 1.6 per cent in Asia on Wednesday (Nov 4) and was trading around US$76,600 as of 10.30 am in Singapore.
The modest move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar, while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington.
For crypto investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms.
More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Friday and Monday while investors sought greater downside protection in options markets ahead of the US elections.

BITCOIN edged lower as bets on a possible Democratic sweep of Congress gained traction , adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite.
For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment.
Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom.
Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets.
The original cryptocurrency slipped as much as 1.6 per cent in Asia on Wednesday (Nov 4) and was trading around US$76,600 as of 10.30 am in Singapore.
The modest move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar, while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington.
For crypto investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms.
More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Friday and Monday while investors sought greater downside protection in options markets ahead of the US elections.

The broader macroeconomic implications are less clear: Political stalemate could limit further fiscal stimulus and weigh on speculative assets, though lower Treasury yields could eventually provide support by easing financial conditions. Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets. “Overall sentiment in crypto is near-term moderate fear and long-term uncertainty,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “Near-term fear because it is still tracking overall risk assets, and with the tech selloff and potentially a restart to the war in the Middle East that is causing some downward pressure.” Democrats had been widely expected to take control of the House of Representatives, with a chance of also taking the Senate, putting them at odds with President Donald Trump’s Republican White House. The Trump family’s financial gains from its crypto ventures became a contentious issue this year, helping derail a regulatory bill seen as critical to the industry. “With the Clarity Act already stalled in the Senate, a change in committee control would most likely mean renegotiation rather than a quick revival, and markets had largely priced that in,” Lucas said. passages: American Bitcoin Corp. (Nasdaq: ABTC) reported about $126 million in third-quarter net income on Wednesday, a swing from a $57.2 million loss in the prior quarter that rested largely on a $197.3 million gain on the company’s bitcoin holdings rather than on mining revenue.
American Bitcoin said it sold a portion of production to cover operating costs while still adding to its strategic reserve.
Holdings rose by about 425 bitcoin, or about 5%, to roughly 8,427 as of Sept.
That total includes about 3,090 bitcoin pledged for miner purchases under agreements with Bitmain.
The owned fleet stood at about 89,242 bitcoin miners with roughly 28.1 EH/s of capacity at quarter-end.
Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. helped launch the venture with Hut 8 in 2025; earlier Bitcoin Magazine coverage has put the Trump family’s stake near 20%, with Hut 8 holding the rest.
The company has climbed the corporate treasury ranks as it stacked coins after its Nasdaq debut.
At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is above $80,500 and shares of American Bitcoin were down over 5.5% today.
Bitcoin Magazine is published by BTC Inc., a subsidiary of Nakamoto Inc. (NASDAQ: NAKA).
Gross profit was about $25.8 million, a 41% margin, compared with about $33.0 million and 49% a quarter earlier, as seasonal power costs rose across its sites.
Whether another quarter of bitcoin price gains can keep paper profits ahead of higher power costs and thinner mining margins is the question the release leaves open.

extraction.body: American Bitcoin Corp. (Nasdaq: ABTC) reported about $126 million in third-quarter net income on Wednesday, a swing from a $57.2 million loss in the prior quarter that rested largely on a $197.3 million gain on the company’s bitcoin holdings rather than on mining revenue. The Miami-based miner and treasury company, a majority-owned subsidiary of Hut 8 Corp. and co-founded with Trump family backing, mined about 891 bitcoin in the quarter at a cost of roughly $42,100 each and ended September with about 8,427 BTC. Mining revenue was about $63.4 million, down from about $67.0 million in the second quarter. Gross profit was about $25.8 million, a 41% margin, compared with about $33.0 million and 49% a quarter earlier, as seasonal power costs rose across its sites. Adjusted EBITDA came in at about $221 million, compared with an Adjusted EBITDA loss of about $45.0 million in the second quarter, according to the company’s release . Eric Trump, co-founder and chief strategy officer of American Bitcoin, said the quarter delivered the net income and Adjusted EBITDA figures while growing the bitcoin reserve and bitcoin per share. Chief Executive Mike Ho said the company kept mining at a structural discount to spot and raised satoshis per share by about 5% without issuing shares through its at-the-market program or buying bitcoin on the open market. The income statement makes the driver plain. American Bitcoin booked a $197.3 million gain on digital assets in the third quarter, after a $71.2 million loss on that line in the second. Operating income was about $191.8 million. Other expense included a $64.3 million loss on derivatives. Strip the mark-to-market move out of the picture and the operating story looks quieter. Revenue per bitcoin mined was about $71,100, down slightly from about $71,900 in the second quarter, and the cost to mine rose to about $42,100 from about $36,500, the company said. Production of about 891 bitcoin was below the second quarter’s roughly 932 coins, which the company had called its highest quarterly haul on record when it reported a $57.2 million second-quarter loss alongside a climb in holdings to about 8,002 BTC. American Bitcoin said it sold a portion of production to cover operating costs while still adding to its strategic reserve. Holdings rose by about 425 bitcoin, or about 5%, to roughly 8,427 as of Sept. 30. That total includes about 3,090 bitcoin pledged for miner purchases under agreements with Bitmain. Management’s preferred yardstick is satoshis per share, which rose about 5% to roughly 11,572 from about 10,989 at the end of June. The share count reflects a 1-for-15 reverse stock split effected earlier this year on July 2. The owned fleet stood at about 89,242 bitcoin miners with roughly 28.1 EH/s of capacity at quarter-end. American Bitcoin remains majority-owned by Hut 8, which on the same day reported its own third-quarter results and confirmed bitcoin sales used to fund share buybacks while shifting mining into the American Bitcoin vehicle. Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. helped launch the venture with Hut 8 in 2025; earlier Bitcoin Magazine coverage has put the Trump family’s stake near 20%, with Hut 8 holding the rest. The company has climbed the corporate treasury ranks as it stacked coins after its Nasdaq debut. Whether another quarter of bitcoin price gains can keep paper profits ahead of higher power costs and thinner mining margins is the question the release leaves open. extraction.body: American Bitcoin Corp. (Nasdaq: ABTC) reported about $126 million in third-quarter net income on Wednesday, a swing from a $57.2 million loss in the prior quarter that rested largely on a $197.3 million gain on the company’s bitcoin holdings rather than on mining revenue. The Miami-based miner and treasury company, a majority-owned subsidiary of Hut 8 Corp. and co-founded with Trump family backing, mined about 891 bitcoin in the quarter at a cost of roughly $42,100 each and ended September with about 8,427 BTC. Mining revenue was about $63.4 million, down from about $67.0 million in the second quarter. Gross profit was about $25.8 million, a 41% margin, compared with about $33.0 million and 49% a quarter earlier, as seasonal power costs rose across its sites. Adjusted EBITDA came in at about $221 million, compared with an Adjusted EBITDA loss of about $45.0 million in the second quarter, according to the company’s release . Eric Trump, co-founder and chief strategy officer of American Bitcoin, said the quarter delivered the net income and Adjusted EBITDA figures while growing the bitcoin reserve and bitcoin per share. Chief Executive Mike Ho said the company kept mining at a structural discount to spot and raised satoshis per share by about 5% without issuing shares through its at-the-market program or buying bitcoin on the open market. The income statement makes the driver plain. American Bitcoin booked a $197.3 million gain on digital assets in the third quarter, after a $71.2 million loss on that line in the second. Operating income was about $191.8 million. Other expense included a $64.3 million loss on derivatives. Strip the mark-to-market move out of the picture and the operating story looks quieter. Revenue per bitcoin mined was about $71,100, down slightly from about $71,900 in the second quarter, and the cost to mine rose to about $42,100 from about $36,500, the company said. Production of about 891 bitcoin was below the second quarter’s roughly 932 coins, which the company had called its highest quarterly haul on record when it reported a $57.2 million second-quarter loss alongside a climb in holdings to about 8,002 BTC. American Bitcoin said it sold a portion of production to cover operating costs while still adding to its strategic reserve. Holdings rose by about 425 bitcoin, or about 5%, to roughly 8,427 as of Sept. 30. That total includes about 3,090 bitcoin pledged for miner purchases under agreements with Bitmain. Management’s preferred yardstick is satoshis per share, which rose about 5% to roughly 11,572 from about 10,989 at the end of June. The share count reflects a 1-for-15 reverse stock split effected earlier this year on July 2. The owned fleet stood at about 89,242 bitcoin miners with roughly 28.1 EH/s of capacity at quarter-end. American Bitcoin remains majority-owned by Hut 8, which on the same day reported its own third-quarter results and confirmed bitcoin sales used to fund share buybacks while shifting mining into the American Bitcoin vehicle. Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. helped launch the venture with Hut 8 in 2025; earlier Bitcoin Magazine coverage has put the Trump family’s stake near 20%, with Hut 8 holding the rest. The company has climbed the corporate treasury ranks as it stacked coins after its Nasdaq debut. Whether another quarter of bitcoin price gains can keep paper profits ahead of higher power costs and thinner mining margins is the question the release leaves open. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is above $80,500 and shares of American Bitcoin were down over 5.5% today. Watch live, catch up on episodes, and get exclusive content on the go. sources.title: Nothing’s first AI device will have no screen — and launches in December - Notebookcheck
passages: Nothing is preparing to launch its first AI-native device in December, and CEO Carl Pei says it will have no screen.
Pei has offered few details about the upcoming product, but describes it as a standalone tool rather than another AI-powered app.

Pei announced the launch in a post on X, describing the device as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.” He added that it “has no screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Nothing has not disclosed the product’s form, features, price, or exact launch date.
The only concrete detail is the absence of a display, alongside a teaser image showing the Nothing logo and an ambiguous black rounded corner.
The announcement comes a little over a year after Pei first outlined Nothing’s plans for AI-native devices and an AI operating system.
There have been rumors that Nothing is developing two pairs of AI smart glasses , one of which reportedly will not have cameras.
Screen-free AI devices are not entirely new, with products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend already attempting to bring AI assistants into standalone gadgets.

sources.title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test - Ars Technica
passages: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs.
Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one?
The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.
With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone.
While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini.
Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable.
Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.
On the software front, the device will offer a choice.
You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose.
It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser).
The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months?
If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it.

Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics. The company’s cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it’s probably “enough” for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off. On the software front, the device will offer a choice. You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose. It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser). Some minor details are still up in the air. The designers aren’t yet sure about waterproofing and durability ratings, and the battery capacity could change. But they hope that spec will go up, not down, if it changes at all. Carrier support is also unclear right now. It will be an unlocked 5G phone, and the company is aiming for “broad global support.” But if you’re on a restrictive carrier like Verizon, you may be out of luck. The other wrinkle is the timeline. The Enough Phone goes live on Kickstarter today , with shipping currently slated for May 2027. The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months? Plenty of Kickstarter projects have failed to deliver on time (or at all). The Enough Phone team points out that this isn’t its first smartphone effort, though. The team says it has designed and shipped hardware for other companies you’ve heard of, working as an original design manufacturer (ODM). If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it. The Enough Phone starts at $399 for early backers. It will go up to $449 and then $499 later. The final MSRP will be $599. That’s not bad for a niche piece of hardware, given the rapid increase in component costs. You will have to take a little leap of faith to get on board with the Enough Phone. The company says it plans to support the device with updates through 2032, which is almost flagship territory. But when a company like Samsung or Google makes that commitment, it’s essentially a guarantee. This is the first phone this group has made under its own brand, and there’s no telling how that will work out. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. sources.title: Enough Phone Review: $399 Small Android Worth It? [2026] - shattered.io
passages: A compact Android handset called the Enough Phone is asking the question the phone industry keeps dodging: will people really pay for a small phone?
The two products share almost nothing beyond being phones, and that contrast shows how wide the market has grown.
One end sells cutting-edge complexity at $1,999.
If enough people pledge, production goes ahead.
That structure suits a niche, and it explains why the small-phone idea now surfaces mostly from independent teams.
At that price, the phone competes with well-reviewed mid-range models from established brands, and those carry warranties, carrier support and retail returns.
It suggests text will look clean enough for daily use but will not match the densest panels on premium phones.
Memory pricing pressure squeezes margins even at the largest companies, a theme we explored in our report on Mac sales and memory costs .
A small firm that wants to ship 8GB of RAM at $399 faces those same costs without Apple’s buying power.
For wider context on devices and components, our hardware section collects related coverage.
Most current phones run larger than 5.3 inches, so small-phone shoppers have few new options.
Reports put the early Kickstarter price at $399 and the planned regular price at $599.
The reporting identifies the maker only as the company, and its official name is unconfirmed, a gap that matters to anyone weighing a crowdfunding pledge.
That is a $200 gap, or about 33 percent off the regular price for people who commit early.
For that money, the spec list reads well, and the discount rewards the people who carry the risk.
Whether it is sustainable is another matter, and without financial disclosures we cannot judge the company’s margins.
The phone runs Android, and reports mention compatibility with OdysseyOS.
Small phones have a long and frustrating record.
That outcome gave the industry its lesson: people say they want small phones, but they often buy bigger ones when the moment comes.
A single crowdfunded phone will not shift global smartphone share.
A strong campaign would encourage other small brands and perhaps nudge larger makers to test compact variants again.
A weak one would reinforce the view that small-phone enthusiasm is mostly talk.

coreStoryFacts.text: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs.
Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one?
The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.
With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone.
While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini.
Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable.
Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.
On the software front, the device will offer a choice.
You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose.
It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser).
The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months?
If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it.

extraction.body: It won’t win the specs race, but it will actually fit in your hand. The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics. The company’s cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it’s probably “enough” for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off. On the software front, the device will offer a choice. You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose. It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser). Some minor details are still up in the air. The designers aren’t yet sure about waterproofing and durability ratings, and the battery capacity could change. But they hope that spec will go up, not down, if it changes at all. Carrier support is also unclear right now. It will be an unlocked 5G phone, and the company is aiming for “broad global support.” But if you’re on a restrictive carrier like Verizon, you may be out of luck. The other wrinkle is the timeline. The Enough Phone goes live on Kickstarter today , with shipping currently slated for May 2027. The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months? Plenty of Kickstarter projects have failed to deliver on time (or at all). The Enough Phone team points out that this isn’t its first smartphone effort, though. The team says it has designed and shipped hardware for other companies you’ve heard of, working as an original design manufacturer (ODM). If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it. The Enough Phone starts at $399 for early backers. It will go up to $449 and then $499 later. The final MSRP will be $599. That’s not bad for a niche piece of hardware, given the rapid increase in component costs. You will have to take a little leap of faith to get on board with the Enough Phone. The company says it plans to support the device with updates through 2032, which is almost flagship territory. But when a company like Samsung or Google makes that commitment, it’s essentially a guarantee. This is the first phone this group has made under its own brand, and there’s no telling how that will work out. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
