extraction.body: A compact Android handset called the Enough Phone is asking the question the phone industry keeps dodging: will people really pay for a small phone? According to coverage from Ars Technica and 9to5Google, the device pairs a 5.3-inch display with a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, all inside a body that measures 132.8 x 63.8 x 12mm. Reports put the early Kickstarter price at $399 and the planned regular price at $599. Shipping is reported to begin in May 2027. The reporting identifies the maker only as the company, and its official name is unconfirmed, a gap that matters to anyone weighing a crowdfunding pledge. The timing stands out. Flagship launches keep climbing in size and price, as our look at the $1,999 iPhone Duo supply gap shows. The Enough Phone runs the opposite direction, and it will test whether the loud online demand for small phones turns into paid preorders. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The story comes down to a handful of reported facts. The Enough Phone is a compact Android phone with a 5.3-inch LCD, offered through Kickstarter, with preorder availability reported. Coverage describes a polycarbonate body, a fingerprint sensor built into the power button, and a battery that owners can swap themselves. Several details remain open. Reporting says the specifications were still being finalized, so the final battery capacity, the exact software-update terms and the final shipping date all stay unconfirmed. One report gives April 2027 as the delivery month, while the majority of the coverage says May 2027. We treat May 2027 as the working date and April as conflicting. Size is the headline feature. A 5.3-inch screen sits well below the large panels that dominate current shelves, and it lets the phone slip into a pocket without a second thought. The maker is betting that a visible slice of buyers will accept trade-offs elsewhere to get that. The reported resolution is 1,520 x 720, or roughly 1.09 million pixels. Our arithmetic from the stated figures gives a diagonal of about 1,682 pixels, which works out to around 317 pixels per inch on a 5.3-inch panel. That is our calculation, not a figure the company published. It suggests text will look clean enough for daily use but will not match the densest panels on premium phones. The 1,520 x 720 grid also implies a tall aspect ratio of roughly 19 to 9. That shape keeps the phone narrow, which helps one-handed use. A wider screen of the same diagonal would force a wider body. The user-replaceable battery is the feature most likely to win hearts among repair-minded buyers. Reporting estimates the capacity at 3,500 to 4,000mAh but flags that number as unconfirmed because the specifications were still being finalized. Treat both ends of the range as provisional. Capacity matters less here than the ability to swap the cell. A battery wears out first on almost every phone, and a replaceable one extends useful life by years without a repair shop visit. It also lets travelers carry a spare. That fits with the reported software support through 2032, since a phone that can get a new battery and fresh updates can plausibly last that long. The industry is moving the other way. Leaks around the next iPhone point to a bigger battery inside a sealed body, as we noted in our coverage of the iPhone 18 battery and price leak . Big makers chase battery life through larger cells. The Enough Phone chases longevity through access. Both are answers to the same worry, but they appeal to different buyers. The 12mm thickness is the cost. A removable back, a polycarbonate shell and a user-serviceable cell all add bulk. Polycarbonate also signals a trade-off in feel, since it lacks the glass or metal finish of premium phones. It does tend to survive drops better and costs less, which suits the price target. Reports give two prices. Early Kickstarter backers can reportedly pay $399, and the planned regular price is $599. That is a $200 gap, or about 33 percent off the regular price for people who commit early. The $599 figure is the more interesting one. At that price, the phone competes with well-reviewed mid-range models from established brands, and those carry warranties, carrier support and retail returns. A buyer paying $599 for a small phone is paying for the form factor and the repair story, not for raw specifications. That is a narrower market than the loud online chatter suggests. The $399 backer rate looks more competitive. For that money, the spec list reads well, and the discount rewards the people who carry the risk. Whether it is sustainable is another matter, and without financial disclosures we cannot judge the company’s margins. Crowdfunding a phone is hard. A backer pays months before delivery, and the product can change between pledge and shipment. Here, reporting says the specifications are still being finalized, and the official company name is unconfirmed. Those two facts are the main risk flags. The May 2027 target gives the team roughly six months from today. That is a short runway for a hardware product with a custom body, a removable battery and a software stack. Kickstarter campaigns in consumer electronics frequently slip, and while we cannot say this one will, backers should plan for the possibility. The April versus May discrepancy already shows how soft the date is. Prospective backers can cut their risk with a few checks: None of this means the project will fail. It means the usual crowdfunding caution applies with extra force when basic facts like the company name are not yet public. The phone runs Android, and reports mention compatibility with OdysseyOS. The material available does not explain what that compatibility means in practice, so we will not guess. It could refer to an alternative operating system option or to a software layer. Until the company says more, treat it as an open question. Support through 2032 is the other headline. Reported support through that year would amount to roughly five years after the reported ship date, a long stretch for a mid-range phone from a small firm. The exact update policy is unconfirmed, though. Backers should look for specifics: how many major Android versions, how often security patches arrive, and who delivers them. A promise of support through a date means little without those terms in writing. Niche Android hardware has a track record of carving out loyal audiences when it offers something big brands skip. The Redmagic 12 Pro and its Linux terminal shows one such angle for power users. The Enough Phone targets a different crowd, people who want a small phone they can repair, but the playbook is similar: serve a specific group very well. Direct spec-for-spec rivals are scarce, which is the point of the product. Most current phones run larger than 5.3 inches, so small-phone shoppers have few new options. We avoid quoting rival specifications here because they fall outside the verified material for this story. A price-ladder view is still possible using figures we have already reported on this site. The iPhone Duo costs about 3.3 times the Enough Phone’s planned regular price and about five times its backer price. The two products share almost nothing beyond being phones, and that contrast shows how wide the market has grown. One end sells cutting-edge complexity at $1,999. The other sells simplicity at $399 to $599. Foldables solve the big-screen-in-a-small-body puzzle with hinges and cost. Demand for them is real, as shown by a 20 percent plus week-on-week sales rise for the Galaxy Z Fold8 in Korea, which we covered in our Galaxy Z Fold8 sales report . The Enough Phone attacks the pocket problem from the other side. It makes the screen small and keeps the price low, with no hinge to break. A buyer who wants a phone that vanishes into a pocket and still runs modern apps has few choices today. That gap is the product’s best argument. Whether the gap is large enough to support a business is the open question. Small phones have a long and frustrating record. Earlier this decade, Apple tried compact iPhones with its mini models, then dropped the line after two generations, with industry reports pointing to weak sales relative to larger models. That outcome gave the industry its lesson: people say they want small phones, but they often buy bigger ones when the moment comes. The pattern repeats across the market. Online comment threads fill with requests for compact phones, yet sales data from major makers has rarely rewarded the segment. A few reasons recur. Larger screens help with video and gaming, and bigger bodies hold bigger batteries. Makers also face the same engineering and marketing costs for a small phone as for a large one, and they earn less per unit. The Enough Phone enters with a different model. A crowdfunding campaign measures demand before the company builds in volume. If enough people pledge, production goes ahead. If not, the cost of being wrong stays smaller than it would for a large manufacturer. That structure suits a niche, and it explains why the small-phone idea now surfaces mostly from independent teams. Repairability adds a second historical thread. Replaceable batteries were standard on phones for many years before sealed designs took over. By bringing the feature back, the Enough Phone ties two nostalgic wishes together: smaller size and user control. The immediate market impact is small. A single crowdfunded phone will not shift global smartphone share. The effect that matters is informational. The pledge total, once public, will give the industry a rare data point on paid demand for compact hardware, as opposed to the free demand voiced in comments. Two outcomes would carry weight. A strong campaign would encourage other small brands and perhaps nudge larger makers to test compact variants again. A weak one would reinforce the view that small-phone enthusiasm is mostly talk. Either way, the campaign works as a live experiment, and we will track the result. Supply costs form the backdrop. Memory pricing pressure squeezes margins even at the largest companies, a theme we explored in our report on Mac sales and memory costs . A small firm that wants to ship 8GB of RAM at $399 faces those same costs without Apple’s buying power. For wider context on devices and components, our hardware section collects related coverage. These are our analysis, not reported facts. We offer them so readers can judge how the story may play out. One report gives April 2027 as the delivery month, while the majority of the coverage says May 2027. We treat May 2027 as the working date and April as conflicting.

Size is the headline feature. A 5.3-inch screen sits well below the large panels that dominate current shelves, and it lets the phone slip into a pocket without a second thought. The maker is betting that a visible slice of buyers will accept trade-offs elsewhere to get that.

The reported resolution is 1,520 x 720, or roughly 1.09 million pixels. Our arithmetic from the stated figures gives a diagonal of about 1,682 pixels, which works out to around 317 pixels per inch on a 5.3-inch panel. That is our calculation, not a figure the company published. It suggests text will look clean enough for daily use but will not match the densest panels on premium phones.
The 1,520 x 720 grid also implies a tall aspect ratio of roughly 19 to 9. That shape keeps the phone narrow, which helps one-handed use. A wider screen of the same diagonal would force a wider body.

The user-replaceable battery is the feature most likely to win hearts among repair-minded buyers. Reporting estimates the capacity at 3,500 to 4,000mAh but flags that number as unconfirmed because the specifications were still being finalized. Treat both ends of the range as provisional.

Capacity matters less here than the ability to swap the cell. A battery wears out first on almost every phone, and a replaceable one extends useful life by years without a repair shop visit. It also lets travelers carry a spare. That fits with the reported software support through 2032, since a phone that can get a new battery and fresh updates can plausibly last that long.

The industry is moving the other way. Leaks around the next iPhone point to a bigger battery inside a sealed body, as we noted in our coverage of the iPhone 18 battery and price leak . Big makers chase battery life through larger cells. The Enough Phone chases longevity through access. Both are answers to the same worry, but they appeal to different buyers.

The 12mm thickness is the cost. A removable back, a polycarbonate shell and a user-serviceable cell all add bulk. Polycarbonate also signals a trade-off in feel, since it lacks the glass or metal finish of premium phones. It does tend to survive drops better and costs less, which suits the price target.

Reports give two prices. Early Kickstarter backers can reportedly pay $399, and the planned regular price is $599. That is a $200 gap, or about 33 percent off the regular price for people who commit early.

The $599 figure is the more interesting one. At that price, the phone competes with well-reviewed mid-range models from established brands, and those carry warranties, carrier support and retail returns. A buyer paying $599 for a small phone is paying for the form factor and the repair story, not for raw specifications. That is a narrower market than the loud online chatter suggests.

The $399 backer rate looks more competitive. For that money, the spec list reads well, and the discount rewards the people who carry the risk. Whether it is sustainable is another matter, and without financial disclosures we cannot judge the company’s margins.

Crowdfunding a phone is hard. A backer pays months before delivery, and the product can change between pledge and shipment. Here, reporting says the specifications are still being finalized, and the official company name is unconfirmed. Those two facts are the main risk flags.

The May 2027 target gives the team roughly six months from today. That is a short runway for a hardware product with a custom body, a removable battery and a software stack. Kickstarter campaigns in consumer electronics frequently slip, and while we cannot say this one will, backers should plan for the possibility. The April versus May discrepancy already shows how soft the date is.
Prospective backers can cut their risk with a few checks:
None of this means the project will fail. It means the usual crowdfunding caution applies with extra force when basic facts like the company name are not yet public.

The phone runs Android, and reports mention compatibility with OdysseyOS. The material available does not explain what that compatibility means in practice, so we will not guess. It could refer to an alternative operating system option or to a software layer. Until the company says more, treat it as an open question.

Support through 2032 is the other headline. Reported support through that year would amount to roughly five years after the reported ship date, a long stretch for a mid-range phone from a small firm. The exact update policy is unconfirmed, though. Backers should look for specifics: how many major Android versions, how often security patches arrive, and who delivers them. A promise of support through a date means little without those terms in writing.

Niche Android hardware has a track record of carving out loyal audiences when it offers something big brands skip. The Redmagic 12 Pro and its Linux terminal shows one such angle for power users. The Enough Phone targets a different crowd, people who want a small phone they can repair, but the playbook is similar: serve a specific group very well.

Direct spec-for-spec rivals are scarce, which is the point of the product. Most current phones run larger than 5.3 inches, so small-phone shoppers have few new options. We avoid quoting rival specifications here because they fall outside the verified material for this story. A price-ladder view is still possible using figures we have already reported on this site.

The iPhone Duo costs about 3.3 times the Enough Phone’s planned regular price and about five times its backer price. The two products share almost nothing beyond being phones, and that contrast shows how wide the market has grown. One end sells cutting-edge complexity at $1,999. The other sells simplicity at $399 to $599.

Foldables solve the big-screen-in-a-small-body puzzle with hinges and cost. Demand for them is real, as shown by a 20 percent plus week-on-week sales rise for the Galaxy Z Fold8 in Korea, which we covered in our Galaxy Z Fold8 sales report . The Enough Phone attacks the pocket problem from the other side. It makes the screen small and keeps the price low, with no hinge to break.

A buyer who wants a phone that vanishes into a pocket and still runs modern apps has few choices today. That gap is the product’s best argument. Whether the gap is large enough to support a business is the open question.

Small phones have a long and frustrating record. Earlier this decade, Apple tried compact iPhones with its mini models, then dropped the line after two generations, with industry reports pointing to weak sales relative to larger models. That outcome gave the industry its lesson: people say they want small phones, but they often buy bigger ones when the moment comes.

The pattern repeats across the market. Online comment threads fill with requests for compact phones, yet sales data from major makers has rarely rewarded the segment. A few reasons recur. Larger screens help with video and gaming, and bigger bodies hold bigger batteries. Makers also face the same engineering and marketing costs for a small phone as for a large one, and they earn less per unit.

The Enough Phone enters with a different model. A crowdfunding campaign measures demand before the company builds in volume. If enough people pledge, production goes ahead. If not, the cost of being wrong stays smaller than it would for a large manufacturer. That structure suits a niche, and it explains why the small-phone idea now surfaces mostly from independent teams.

Repairability adds a second historical thread. Replaceable batteries were standard on phones for many years before sealed designs took over. By bringing the feature back, the Enough Phone ties two nostalgic wishes together: smaller size and user control.

The immediate market impact is small. A single crowdfunded phone will not shift global smartphone share. The effect that matters is informational. The pledge total, once public, will give the industry a rare data point on paid demand for compact hardware, as opposed to the free demand voiced in comments.

Two outcomes would carry weight. A strong campaign would encourage other small brands and perhaps nudge larger makers to test compact variants again. A weak one would reinforce the view that small-phone enthusiasm is mostly talk. Either way, the campaign works as a live experiment, and we will track the result.

Supply costs form the backdrop. Memory pricing pressure squeezes margins even at the largest companies, a theme we explored in our report on Mac sales and memory costs . A small firm that wants to ship 8GB of RAM at $399 faces those same costs without Apple’s buying power. For wider context on devices and components, our hardware section collects related coverage.
These are our analysis, not reported facts. We offer them so readers can judge how the story may play out.

It is a compact Android phone with a 5.3-inch LCD, a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. It is offered through Kickstarter, according to coverage from Ars Technica and 9to5Google.

extraction.body: HONG KONG -- Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city’s once-thriving pro-democracy movement. Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty to the offense, a move that can typically reduce the sentence. The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city’s biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027. Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong’s offense was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited. He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea. Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears. The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction. Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just teenager, he possessed “big-picture thinking” that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement, she said. “At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment,” she said. Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down , and dozens of civil society groups dissolved . Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism. “NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law. But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city’s stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based. The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019. After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries’ attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said. His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release. His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking. To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997. Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp. extraction.body: HONG KONG -- Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city’s once-thriving pro-democracy movement. Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty to the offense, a move that can typically reduce the sentence. The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city’s biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027. Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong’s offense was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited. He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea. Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears. The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction. Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just teenager, he possessed “big-picture thinking” that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement, she said. “At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment,” she said. Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down , and dozens of civil society groups dissolved . Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism. “NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law. But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city’s stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based. The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019. After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries’ attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said. His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release. His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking. To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997. Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp. Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks. SPY’s monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY’s October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth. The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October. The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before : the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle. For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November’s gains in 2002 and 2022. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%. This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. The technology-packed Nasdaq-100 has been choppier. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) hit $762.86 in October but ended the month at $690.49, 9.5% below that peak. It closed at $685.28 on November 3. Early sector responses point to rotation, with groups moving in different directions. The Wall Street Journal reported that defense stocks sold off after Democrats’ midterm gains . A change in congressional control can reshape spending priorities, and the sectors most tied to Washington tend to adjust first, before broad index funds feel much of the shift. Over the long run, Wall Street has tended to come out stronger after midterms. The Dow ETF’s six-for-six record a year out backs that up. The shorter-term lesson from 2018 is that a strong November can turn into a rough December. I’m watching whether SPY holds above its October close of $755.72 through year-end. Falling below the pre-election October close is exactly what happened in December 2018. Equities have historically enjoyed a strong run after midterm elections, and so has crypto in its short existence. Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, was essentially created right after the worst of the 2008 Great Recession, when many people lost faith in the mainstream financial system. It was originally viewed as an alternative currency, although it has since morphed into an investment. This means it has been around for four midterm elections. The end of midterms has historically led to a rally in stocks because it removes uncertainty and provides the market with greater clarity on what policy and regulation could look like during the next two to four years. Crypto is often more volatile than equities, so it's not a huge surprise to learn that Bitcoin, a bellwether for crypto, has performed exceptionally well in the year after midterm elections, according to data from TradingView and CoinDesk: The crypto market was still in its early stages in 2010 and much smaller than it is today. Investors should remember that although history rhymes, it rarely repeats, so this time could certainly be different. However, Republicans have been unable to pass the Clarity Act, which would clear up many regulatory gray areas, such as which regulatory body has jurisdiction over certain cryptocurrencies. That effectively slows supply growth, which is the main reason investors purchase Bitcoin in the first place: its finite supply makes it at least appear to be a form of digital gold, and therefore a potential hedge against inflation. Coincidentally, after Bitcoin's last four halvings, Bitcoin surged for the next 12 to 18 months or so and then fell into a bear market. Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks. SPY’s monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY’s October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth. The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October. The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before : the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle. For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November’s gains in 2002 and 2022. Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%. This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. The technology-packed Nasdaq-100 has been choppier. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) hit $762.86 in October but ended the month at $690.49, 9.5% below that peak. It closed at $685.28 on November 3. Early sector responses point to rotation, with groups moving in different directions. The Wall Street Journal reported that defense stocks sold off after Democrats’ midterm gains . Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks.

SPY’s monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY’s October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth.

The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October.

The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before : the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle.

For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November’s gains in 2002 and 2022.

Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%.

extraction.body: Wed 4 Nov 2026 · 16:32 EST · 3 min read A former FBI supervisory special agent is expected to plead guilty to stealing roughly $1 million in crypto. The coins came from wallets the bureau was watching as part of a counterintelligence investigation. The defendant is Patrick Steven Yaroch. He is set to enter a guilty plea on November 4, 2026, in US District Court in Alexandria, Virginia. The charges relate to the theft of approximately $1 million in digital assets. The wallets involved were tied to a counterintelligence probe targeting adversarial nations. Court records indicate Yaroch held Top Secret clearance. That clearance gave him access to internal FBI systems, where he was able to obtain the seed phrases for the wallets in question. A seed phrase is a string of words that acts as the master key to a crypto wallet. Whoever knows those words controls the funds, with no bank, password reset or customer service line standing in the way. Yaroch allegedly memorized the phrases rather than copying them down, which avoided leaving an obvious paper trail. From there, the records describe about ten unauthorized transfers out of the investigation-linked wallets. The transfers allegedly took place between late 2024 and July 2026. One court filing puts the total of those transfers at approximately $925,426. The broader case describes the haul as roughly $1 million. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime. Between May and June of 2026, Yaroch allegedly consulted ChatGPT about how to invest the stolen funds. He also reportedly asked the chatbot about relocating to a European Union country. Portugal came up by name. The scheme unraveled through a guilty conscience. According to the research findings, Yaroch confessed to a Department of Justice employee, citing feelings of guilt. He was summarily dismissed from the FBI and arrested on July 31, 2026. Investigators have since recovered more than $925,000 in stolen assets from various accounts. That figure lines up closely with the approximately $925,426 in transfers detailed in one filing. Since October 1, a $1,000 crypto basket split equally among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) has lost money. As of November 4, the basket is worth $886.54, down $113.46, or 11.3%. All four coins fell, showing how the October selloff hit the whole market at once.
Here’s how each coin in the basket has performed as of the morning of November 4.

Bitcoin held up best, with its price at $236.98 and a loss of just $13.02. Ethereum and XRP followed, down $25.06 and $29.12, respectively. Solana, however, saw the steepest decline, dropping to just $203.75, a loss of $46.25.

Over the past month, Solana’s performance has been particularly poor. It closed at a high of $120.76 on October 5, then dropped to a low of $91.84 on November 2. Solana now trades 67% below its all-time high of $293.31 from January 2025. XRP trades 63.8% below its own all-time high, and Ethereum trades 50.8% below its $4,946.05 high , both set in 2025.
Putting the full $1,000 into Bitcoin alone would be worth $947.92 today. The same $1,000 in Solana alone would be worth only $814.99.
Despite October’s downturn, early November has brought some relief. All four coins have risen since the October 31 close. Ethereum is up 8%, XRP is up 5.6%, Bitcoin is up 4%, and Solana is up 1.4%.

Even so, every coin trades below breakeven, the price that would bring a piece back to its starting $250. Bitcoin needs a 5.5% gain to reach breakeven, Ethereum needs 11.1%, XRP needs 13.2%, and Solana needs 22.7%.

Solana faces the steepest climb and has shown the weakest bounce so far. It also trades under its 50-day average of $108.61, a figure traders use to gauge the medium-term trend. Bitcoin also stays below its 50-day average of $81,909.

Spreading the $1,000 across four coins cushioned against the worst single pick, but it still trailed the best one. The basket’s $886.54 beat an all-Solana position worth $814.99, though it fell short of an all-Bitcoin position worth $947.92.

The biggest cryptocurrencies tend to move together, so diversifying among them cushions losses but doesn’t prevent them in a market-wide downturn. Bitcoin fell the least of the four, so every dollar moved into the other three made the loss bigger.

Bitcoin’s next test is a close back above its October 1 level of $84,842, which could lift the rest of the basket too. A close below the November 2 low of $76,709 could mean October’s decline still has further to go, and Solana could feel it first.

Since October 1, a $1,000 crypto basket split equally among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) has lost money. As of November 4, the basket is worth $886.54, down $113.46, or 11.3%. All four coins fell, showing how the October selloff hit the whole market at once.
Here’s how each coin in the basket has performed as of the morning of November 4.

Bitcoin held up best, with its price at $236.98 and a loss of just $13.02. Ethereum and XRP followed, down $25.06 and $29.12, respectively. Solana, however, saw the steepest decline, dropping to just $203.75, a loss of $46.25.

Over the past month, Solana’s performance has been particularly poor. It closed at a high of $120.76 on October 5, then dropped to a low of $91.84 on November 2. Solana now trades 67% below its all-time high of $293.31 from January 2025. XRP trades 63.8% below its own all-time high, and Ethereum trades 50.8% below its $4,946.05 high , both set in 2025.
Putting the full $1,000 into Bitcoin alone would be worth $947.92 today. The same $1,000 in Solana alone would be worth only $814.99.
Despite October’s downturn, early November has brought some relief. All four coins have risen since the October 31 close. Ethereum is up 8%, XRP is up 5.6%, Bitcoin is up 4%, and Solana is up 1.4%.

Even so, every coin trades below breakeven, the price that would bring a piece back to its starting $250. Bitcoin needs a 5.5% gain to reach breakeven, Ethereum needs 11.1%, XRP needs 13.2%, and Solana needs 22.7%.

Solana faces the steepest climb and has shown the weakest bounce so far. It also trades under its 50-day average of $108.61, a figure traders use to gauge the medium-term trend. Bitcoin also stays below its 50-day average of $81,909.

Spreading the $1,000 across four coins cushioned against the worst single pick, but it still trailed the best one. The basket’s $886.54 beat an all-Solana position worth $814.99, though it fell short of an all-Bitcoin position worth $947.92.

The biggest cryptocurrencies tend to move together, so diversifying among them cushions losses but doesn’t prevent them in a market-wide downturn. Bitcoin fell the least of the four, so every dollar moved into the other three made the loss bigger.

Bitcoin’s next test is a close back above its October 1 level of $84,842, which could lift the rest of the basket too. A close below the November 2 low of $76,709 could mean October’s decline still has further to go, and Solana could feel it first.
